The module header says the manifest is consumed by release checks and replay workflows (replay_policy/mod.rs:5). A grep finds no runtime reader of *_REPLAY_POLICY_MANIFEST or of the quota.rs labels. Only CostClass reaches CostGuardRequest, and seven workflows each hard-code their own parameters. Observed drift:
- The managed and Store RespondCapability rows declare ManagementDeployment with DEPLOYMENT_QUOTA_V1 and DEPLOYMENT_RESERVE_V1 (role_command_manifest.rs:367-374, :402-409). Both arms only accept NonrootCyclesCapabilityEnvelopeV1 (macros/endpoints/role.rs:521, wasm_store.rs:175-181), which is guarded as ValueTransfer (nonroot_cycles.rs:560-573).
- RetryPoolRefill is labelled ValueTransfer (:203-209), but its paid Cycles Ledger creation is guarded as ManagementDeployment (workflow/deployment.rs:28-31, :60).
- BootstrapStore, RemoveComponent, RemoveSubtree, ImportPoolCanister, ImportPoolCapacity and RetryPoolReset declare deployment quota and reserve labels but reserve no cost guard.
- DEPLOYMENT_RESERVE_V1 is backed by cycle_reservation_cycles = 0 in every deployment guard (deployment.rs:30-50), so it is only a 1T balance floor.
- HandoffPoolCanister is CostClass::None, although it moves a funded canister out of Root control (canister_pool/mod.rs:545-553).
- RootChainKeySigning, RootCanisterSignaturePrepare and IssuerCanisterSignaturePrepare are never passed to any CostGuardRequest.
tests/cost.rs:53-78 checks only that the labels are present.

Recommendation

Make the manifest executable. Map each quota and reserve label to a single const CostGuard policy (class, window, limit, reservation rule), and have the workflows build their CostGuardRequest from the policy looked up by the manifest's command kind. Add a test asserting that every costed row's command kind is reserved by exactly one runtime guard of the same class, and that uncosted rows reserve none. Correct the drifted rows, or remove the labels that have no enforcement.

lowunverifiedr2-replay-manifest-conformance-5 · robustness · medium confidence
Every control-plane deployment cost guard uses Root itself as the quota subject, so one Component's allocations consume the root-wide per-minute deployment budget of every other Component
crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/deployment.rs:38

Failure scenario

An index or sharding Component churns placement children, allocating and recycling more than 64 per minute. Every other Component's child allocation on the same root fails QuotaExceeded in each window, so their placements and top-level installs stall for as long as the churn continues. The DEPLOYMENT_QUOTA_V1 label suggests a bounded per-operation quota, but the actual bound is shared across all Components.

reserve_component_pool_claim_guard, reserve_component_child_pool_claim_guard, reserve_component_child_install_cost_guard, reserve_component_install_cost_guard and reserve_canister_pool_creation_cost_guard all pass quota_subject = payer = IcOps::canister_self() (deployment.rs:28-51). The limit is MAX_CONTROL_PLANE_DEPLOYMENT_OPERATIONS_PER_WINDOW = 64 per 60 s window (deployment.rs:16-17). The quota key is class, command kind, subject and bucket (ops/cost_guard.rs:352-364), so there is one shared budget per command kind for the whole root. Component-driven child allocations reach these guards through ProvisionChild, ProvisionCanister and AllocatePlacementChild (component_installation/mod.rs:111, :564, :607). A Component can loop allocations and recycles (RecycleCanister returns the child to the pool), staying within its descendant limit indefinitely. Other Components' allocations then fail with CAPACITY_LIMIT and their drivers retry every 1 s (cp-registry-workflow-4).

Recommendation

Key the Component-driven deployment quotas by the requesting Component (or its parent canister) and keep a separate root-wide ceiling. Alternatively, reserve a per-Component share, so one member cannot exhaust the root-wide window. State the chosen subject in the manifest row.

lowconfirmedr2-restart-driver-resumption-5 · liveness · medium confidence

crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/fleet_coordinator/mod.rs:1165

Failure scenario

The Root driver records progress, but record_failure or clear_failure returns Err, for example after a duplicate chain created by a Reconcile re-send or post-upgrade resume changed the record. The driver traps and its chain ends. The Root's status shows a non-terminal phase with no last_failure, so observed_root_failure reports nothing. The Coordinator loop re-queries the Root back-to-back with zero delay, paying for an inter-canister call and full history validation each time. Provisioning never advances until an operator happens to upgrade the Root.

The Root driver advance_scheduled_provisioning traps after the phase's awaits whenever its evidence writes fail: `clear_failure(...).unwrap_or_else(|error| ic_cdk::trap(...))` (component_provisioning.rs:323-325), `error.provisioning_failure().expect("failure context")` and the record_failure trap (348-353). Its chain is a RemoveWhenStopped Once (190-201), so a trap kills it. The only automatic re-arm is resume_after_restart, called solely from Root post_upgrade (component_provisioning.rs:180-188; api/lifecycle.rs:977). After recording root acceptance, the Coordinator reaches the Root through advance_component_root_provisioning. For both Invoke and Reconcile dispositions, that only calls advance_root_component_provisioning, which is just query_root_component_provisioning (fleet_coordinator/mod.rs:1149-1173, 1266-1275). ProvisionComponents is sent only from accept_root_component_provisioning in the acceptance phase (1191-1215). When the Root status is unchanged and has no failure, the Coordinator reschedules with component_provisioning_retry_delay, which is Duration::ZERO unless estate funding is required (930-938, 976-986).

Recommendation

When the Root status shows no progress across polls, have the Coordinator re-send the idempotent ProvisionComponents acceptance, which calls accept_and_schedule (deduplicate that on the Root). Alternatively, give the Root driver a watchdog. Replace the evidence-write traps with typed failures that keep rescheduling, and add a minimum backoff to the Coordinator's no-progress reschedule.

Severity adjusted from medium to low during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): The structural gap is real. After acceptance, advance_component_provisioning_root_acceptance returns Current, and both Invoke and Reconcile only query the Root (fleet_coordinator/mod.rs:1149-1173, 1266-1275). ProvisionComponents is sent only at 1191-1215. The Root chain is re-armed only by resume_after_restart in post_upgrade (component_provisioning.rs:177-188). The cited triggers are wrong, though. First, expect("failure context") cannot fail, because with_provisioning_failure always sets the context when it is absent (canic-core error.rs:85-96). Second, clear_failure and record_failure fail only on a missing or corrupt record or a plan_hash mismatch (failure/mod.rs:46-105). Their read-modify-write runs synchronously after the last await, so duplicate chains cannot race them, and time_is_current holds because IC time is monotonic. Third, an unchanged status does not poll at zero delay. strictly_advances_to requires next != self (component_provisioning_root_progress/mod.rs:91), so validate_root_provision_response returns conflict (reconciliation/mod.rs:238-244), and the Err branch retries after 1 s (fleet_coordinator/mod.rs:967-971). What remains is a trap in schedule_provisioning from ic-timers 64-registration exhaustion or from instruction exhaustion. That needs heavy registry pressure, and a Root upgrade recovers it. Low.

After a subtree restore, index placement re-creates children for keys bound after the backup under new, time-derived operation IDs, so Root pays for duplicates and the original children remain registered with Root but unreachable
crates/canic-core/src/workflow/placement/index/state.rs:115

Failure scenario

Parent P has index pool `users`. P is backed up at T0. At T1, user U is bound to new child C2, which accumulates U's data. At T2, P is restored from T0. At T3, resolve_or_create(users, U) claims again with a new timestamp claim_id, and Root creates C3, paying the creation fee and initial cycles. U is now routed to an empty C3. C2 stays Active in Root's Component Registry, keeps receiving directory syncs and top-ups, and holds one maximum_instances_per_parent slot. Restore touches only manifest members (crates/canic-backup/src/restore/plan/members.rs:17-58). Backup targets come from the last converged ensure topology (crates/canic-cli/src/backup/create/mod.rs:34-36), so children created after the backup are never rolled back. The restored parent's stable index registry has no entry for such a key. resolve_or_create falls through to claim_and_create_instance (index/mod.rs:153-157; create.rs:91-92), which mints claim_id = now_millis.rotate_left(21) ^ nonce (state.rs:115-118). The allocation operation ID hashes that claim_id (model/placement/allocation.rs:59-77,139-143), so it differs from the original. Root short-circuits only on an identical operation ID (canic-control-plane/src/workflow/component_registry/mod.rs:1111-1123) and otherwise reserves a new child. Its per-parent count still includes the orphan (mod.rs:1160-1165). Index cleanup recycles only children it references (index/cleanup.rs:74-94), and nothing reconciles Root's children of the parent with its index. Separately, a pending claim kept in the snapshot whose child was removed later fails recover_child forever: terminal_child_allocation_binding returns invariant when registered_parent is None (component_registry/mod.rs:1260-1263). Scaling and sharding use state-derived sequences and do not diverge this way.

Make index claims converge after a restore. Before minting a claim, ask Root whether it already holds a committed allocation for (parent, pool, key), which requires Root to index placement allocations by subject. lowunverifiedr2-wire-mirror-agreement-3 · robustness · medium confidence
inspect_message decodes the command unions with candid::decode_one and no quota, so a zero-byte skip bomb runs to the inspect instruction limit before rejection
crates/canic/src/macros/endpoints/root.rs:178

Failure scenario

An anonymous sender submits a 60-byte canic_root_command ingress: variant ImportPoolCanister = record { canister_id; junk: vec null } with junk declared at length 2^32-1. inspect_message loops over 4 billion null elements until it hits the inspect-message instruction limit and traps, and the message is rejected. Each such message costs a node the full inspect budget. Canister cycles are not charged, so the damage is bounded node-side DoS.

Evidence

The root, managed, Coordinator and Store inspect hooks fully decode the command with `::canic::__internal::candid::decode_one::<..>(&bytes)` (root.rs:178, role.rs:577, fleet_coordinator.rs:43-45, wasm_store.rs:44-45). candid::decode_one uses IDLDeserialize::new, which is DecoderConfig::new() with decoding_quota and skipping_quota both None (candid utils.rs:189-197, 300-306; de.rs:46-49, 164-175). add_cost enforces nothing when both quotas are None (de.rs:562-581). Extra wire fields are skipped through deserialize_ignored_any → deserialize_any → deserialize_seq, which iterates the declared length even for zero-byte elements such as null (de.rs:975-984, 1178-1260, 1680-1705). The update path is bounded by skipping_quota(10_000) (expand/mod.rs:333-334). xc-robustness-3 described this as 'only a skipping quota'. In inspect_message there is no quota at all, and the root hook accepts payloads up to about 8.45 MiB (root.rs:172-177).

Recommendation

Decode in inspect_message with a DecoderConfig that sets a small skipping_quota and a decoding_quota proportional to the variant's byte bound, or decode only the variant tag and check the length bound there, leaving full decoding to the update path.

lowunverifiedtests-ci-3 · robustness · high confidence
The `release-commit` recipe runs `git tag` even when `git commit` fails, which leaves the release tag on the pre-release commit.
Makefile:236

Failure scenario

cargo-sort is missing on the maintainer's machine, so the hook fails and `git commit` aborts. v0.110.47 is created on the unbumped validated-source commit, `make release-push` fails, and every later `make release-commit` refuses because the tag exists. The maintainer has to find and delete the stray tag by hand. Pushing it manually would publish a tag on the wrong commit.

Evidence

Makefile:231-237 runs as one `/bin/sh -c` recipe with no `-e`, because the Makefile sets no .SHELLFLAGS. The commands are joined by `;`: `git commit -m "Release $$version"; git tag -a "v$$version" -m ...`. If the commit fails, the shell still runs `git tag`, which tags the current HEAD, the validated source commit that still carries the previous version in Cargo.toml. The recipe's exit status is the tag's, which is 0. The pre-commit hook that `make install-dev` installs runs `make fmt` and can reject a commit (.githooks/pre-commit:39-43, 58-63). `make release-patch` then continues to release-push. check-release-push-ready.sh:18-20 stops the push because HEAD is not the release commit. A retry of `make release-commit` then aborts with "Tag v$version already exists" (Makefile:232-235).

Recommendation

Chain the commands with `&&`, or `set -e` at the start of the recipe, so the tag is created only after a successful commit. Before tagging, also check that `git log -1 --format=%s` equals `Release $version`.

The README says Canic's own cycle and creation operations do not use this builder, so framework invariants are unaffected. A downstream canister that treats every bounded-wait error as a possibly executed call stays correct; it only loses the chance to safely retry clean rejects. The double-payment scenario requires downstream code to wrongly assume PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE means the call did not run. lowunverifiedxc-efficiency-13 · performance · high confidence
Stable records are serde-CBOR with text field-name keys, and [u8; 32] and Vec<u8> fields are encoded as integer arrays, inflating stored bytes and decode cost on every hot scan
crates/canic-core/src/cdk/serialize.rs:31

Failure scenario

Each 32-byte hash costs about 62 bytes stored and 32 per-element visitor calls to decode. Field names add about 10-20 bytes per field. Record sizes grow roughly 1.5-2x, which multiplies the cost of the full-scan paths above (replay receipts, registry entries, sharding assignments) and the effective capacity consumed within each declared byte bound.

All impl_storable_bounded and impl_storable_unbounded records go through ciborium::ser::into_writer and from_reader (cdk/serialize.rs:26-42; cdk/mod.rs:18-80). ciborium encodes structs as maps with text field-name keys, and serde serializes [u8; N] as a tuple and Vec<u8> as a sequence, which CBOR writes one integer per byte (1-2 bytes each). The codebase acknowledges this: 'CBOR encodes a 32-byte `[u8; 32]` key as a two-byte array header followed by at most two bytes per element' (canic-control-plane/src/storage/stable/component_provisioning/mod.rs:36-38). There are 197 `pub ...: [u8; 32]` fields in stable record modules, none using serde_bytes. Replay receipts store response_bytes and staged_response_bytes as Vec<u8> (storage/stable/replay.rs:66-78), and ShardKey stores field names inside every BTree key (storage/stable/sharding/mod.rs:52-71).

Recommendation

Annotate byte arrays and byte vectors with serde_bytes (or wrap them in a ByteBuf newtype), and use compact fixed-layout Storable impls for hot keys. The format is v1 and reinstall-only, so this can be a hard cut.

crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/component_provisioning.rs:353

Failure scenario

1. Provisioning fails with an error whose attached origin (preserved from a retained child failure via `with_observed_provisioning_failure`, component_provisioning.rs:594-599) fails `validate_failure`. Or a concurrent message changes the operation record, so `replace_operation` conflicts. 2. `record_failure` returns Err and the callback traps after its awaits. 3. The provisioning operation stays in its last phase with no retained failure and no scheduled retry. The Coordinator's status polling sees no progress indefinitely. 4. The stuck Running timer makes every PrepareAuthoritySnapshot (Root backup) fail until the Root is upgraded or reinstalled.

Evidence

ic-timers `dispatch_ordinary` marks the entry Running (`begin_ordinary`), awaits the consumer future, and only then calls `complete_ordinary` and removes a `RemoveWhenStopped` entry. There is no Drop guard (ic-timers-0.8.0 runtime/mod.rs:1138-1176). Its README states that `Once` has "No automatic recovery" for traps.

The Root provisioning worker is a `Once` chain (component_provisioning.rs:190-197). After several inter-canister awaits it calls `clear_failure(...).unwrap_or_else(|e| ic_cdk::trap(...))` (line 322-325) and `record_failure(...).unwrap_or_else(|e| ic_cdk::trap(...))` (line 349-353). `record_failure` can fail on a store commit conflict or on `validate_failure` (target, operation id, diagnostic code, retry time), per ops/component_provisioning/failure/mod.rs:46-85 and 170-188. Other drivers (allocation, removal, synchronization) can also trap after awaits through expect/unreachable or instruction exhaustion.

After such a trap:
- No successor is scheduled.
- The only automatic re-arm is `resume_after_restart` (component_provisioning.rs:180-188), called from post_upgrade (api/lifecycle.rs:977).
- `require_root_resumable` rejects any lifecycle identity: it is never in the claimed set, so it yields UnmanagedClaim, and a Running entry yields RunningClaim (workflow/runtime/timer/mod.rs:132-163, 471-484). Root authority snapshots are therefore refused until the heap is reset.

Recommendation

Inside timer callbacks, never trap after the first await. Log the error, retain a typed failure if possible, and reschedule with backoff by returning a TimerRunResult with a retry directive. If an evidence write truly cannot be committed, record a separate minimal "driver fault" marker and let a watchdog reconcile it. Alternatively, move these state machines to a `Watchdog` policy, whose committed successor survives trapped work. Make `require_root_resumable` tolerate stale lifecycle entries, or expose a controller command that re-arms retained operations and prunes dead Running entries without a full restart.

Verifier (confirmed): The mechanism is real, but the triggers the finding names cannot be reached in normal operation. ic-timers-0.8.0 runtime/mod.rs:1138-1176 calls begin_ordinary, awaits the consumer future and only then calls complete_ordinary, with no Drop guard. A trap in a continuation after an await therefore leaves the RemoveWhenStopped entry Running, and no successor is scheduled. Lifecycle identities are never in the claimed set, so require_observed_claims_resumable (timer/mod.rs:471-484) refuses PrepareAuthoritySnapshot (api/lifecycle.rs:141). The Coordinator only polls status (fleet_coordinator/mod.rs:1266-1275), so the Root timer is the only driver. The only re-arm is resume_after_restart in post_upgrade (lifecycle.rs:977). Corrections to the finding: (1) The commit-conflict scenario is refuted. clear_failure and record_failure read `before` themselves and call replace_operation with no await in between (failure/mod.rs:52-83, 93-105). clear_failure also runs right after a synchronous status() that validated the same record, so it cannot fail. (2) validate_failure can fail only when diagnostic_code is 0, operation_id is zero or target is anonymous. Code 0 is not allocatable (diagnostics/mod.rs:79-81). A child-derived origin uses fleet_subnet_root with validated nonzero codes (child_failure/mod.rs:57-66). Reaching it needs a Canic peer bound to Root to forward raw code 0. (3) Recovery exists: upgrading Root with the same build re-arms the driver. While provisioning is active, snapshots are blocked by design anyway. Public update and inspect_message paths decode untrusted Candid with only a skipping quota (no decoding quota), before any access check
crates/canic-macros/src/endpoint/expand/mod.rs:334

Failure scenario

An arbitrary canister repeatedly calls a public update with a payload built to maximize decoding work, for example a long vec of minimal elements or zero-width elements wherever a DTO admits opt/null subtyping. The target canister pays execution cycles for the decode, and possibly up to the 40B-instruction trap, before the access check rejects the caller. The attacker pays only the call fee. The result is bounded cycle drain and DoS against Root, Coordinator or Store.

Evidence

The raw update adapter builds `DecoderConfig::new()` with only `set_skipping_quota(10_000)` and then decodes all arguments (expand/mod.rs:331-345). It then calls the wrapper that runs preflight and access (expand/mod.rs:124-131, 347-351). Non-raw updates use ic-cdk's default, which is also skipping-quota only (ic-cdk-macros-0.20.3 export.rs:258-259). Root and Store inspect_message call `candid::decode_one::<RootCommand>` / `<StoreCommand>` with candid's default config, which has no quotas (root.rs:178, wasm_store.rs:44-45).

In candid 0.10.37, per-element costs are charged only when `decoding_quota` is set (de.rs:562-580), and vec length comes from the wire (de.rs:490-493, 1189). By contrast, the delegated-token and attestation decoders set explicit decoding quotas (access/auth/token.rs:86-90, attestation.rs:42-44).

Public updates such as `canic_root_command`, `canic_coordinator_command`, `canic_wasm_store_command` and `_immutableObjectStorageConfirmBlobDeletion(Vec<Vec<u8>>)` (blob_storage.rs:31-38) can be called by any canister. Inter-canister calls skip inspect_message, and non-raw updates allow payloads up to the 2 MB inter-canister limit.

Recommendation

In the raw adapter and in inspect_message, set `set_decoding_quota(...)` proportional to the method's payload limit, plus `set_max_type_len`. For non-raw public updates, set a decoding quota through the cdk `decode_with` hook or switch them to the raw adapter with an explicit payload limit. For inspect-message pre-decodes, prefer a cheap variant-tag peek over a full decode.

crates/canic-control-plane/src/storage/stable/state/root_wasm_store.rs:141

Failure scenario

If any of these records is moved into `BoundedCell`, a StableBTreeMap, or anything else that calls `to_bytes_checked`, the next write traps unconditionally, because the CBOR length never equals the declared fixed size. That would wedge Root env/state writes. Meanwhile the 16 KB state bound that reviewers assume exists is not enforced.

Evidence

The affected declarations are:
- `impl_storable_bounded!(RootWasmStoreStateRecord, 16_384, true)` (root_wasm_store.rs:141)
- `EnvRecord, 2_048, true` (crates/canic-core/src/storage/stable/env.rs:50)
- `FleetStateRecord, 32, true` (crates/canic-core/src/storage/stable/state/fleet.rs:32)
- `WasmStoreGcStateRecord, 128, true` (crates/canic-control-plane/src/storage/stable/template/gc/mod.rs:40)

`impl_storable_bounded!` serializes with serde/CBOR, so the byte length varies (crates/canic-core/src/cdk/mod.rs:22-51). ic-stable-structures `check_bounds` asserts `actual == max_size` for fixed-size bounds (storable.rs:49-61). crates/canic-core/src/workflow/runtime/auth/prepare/mod.rs:112

Failure scenario

An app follows the docs and treats `token.claims.ext` as issuer-attested data, for example a tenant id or tier, in an endpoint guarded by `auth::authenticated(...)`. An attacker self-prepares a token with ext = <victim tenant> and presents it. The issuer's canister signature verifies, so the attacker gains the victim tenant's context. Separately, an app that declares `my_app:admin` in allowed_scopes and gates admin endpoints on `authenticated("my_app:admin")`, relying on the documented rule that such scopes cannot be self-issued, gives admin access to every principal.

Evidence

The open `canic_command::PrepareDelegatedToken` path copies `ext: request.ext` straight from the caller's request into the prepare input (crates/canic-core/src/workflow/runtime/auth/prepare/mod.rs:108-113). Admission validates only the grants (crates/canic-core/src/workflow/runtime/auth/prepare/admission.rs:108-128), and `prepare_delegated_token` embeds `ext: input.ext` in the claims that the issuer canister-signs (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/delegated/prepare.rs:146-157). Yet docs/architecture/authentication.md:239-240 describes `claims.ext` as "opaque application data set by the issuer, signed as part of DelegatedTokenClaims". For scopes, `public_delegated_token_prepare_scope` self-issues `session`, `verify` and any scope declared in the target role's `local_application_authorization.allowed_scopes` (crates/canic-core/src/domain/policy/pure/auth/mod.rs:142-160). docs/contracts/AUTH_DELEGATED_SIGNATURES.md:287-293 and docs/architecture/authentication.md:711-715 still say public prepare "only self-issues public login scopes: session and verify" and that privileged application scopes need a caller-authorized path. The emitted endpoint gives applications no hook to add their own issuance authorization.

Either reject non-empty `ext` on the public prepare path and add an application-authorized issuance hook for issuer-asserted data, or rewrite AUTH_DELEGATED_SIGNATURES.md, authentication.md and CONFIG.md to state plainly that `ext` and declared application scopes are caller-chosen self-assertions that must never be used as privilege or identity evidence. Add a doc guard test that ties the documented self-issuable scope set to `public_delegated_token_prepare_scope`.

Severity adjusted from medium to low during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): The facts are right, but the scope half is intended behaviour and the ext half is mostly misleading docs. Public prepare copies the caller's `ext` into the claims (prepare/mod.rs:108-113; ops/auth/delegated/prepare.rs:146-157). It also self-issues the scopes declared in `allowed_scopes` (domain/policy/pure/auth/mod.rs:142-160). Scopes: this is the accepted 0.105 design. "public proof/token preparation may request only scopes declared for the target role" (0.105-design.md:399-407). The unit tests cover it, and the 0.105 non-goals say a scope check alone must not authorize mutation (0.105-design.md:104). The canonical docs contradict the code, which is real drift. authentication.md:711-715 and AUTH_DELEGATED_SIGNATURES.md:287-293 still say only `session`/`verify` can be self-issued. CONFIG.md does not document `local_application_authorization` at all. ext: authentication.md:239-240 says it is "set by the issuer". AUTH_DELEGATED_SIGNATURES.md:209-211 only calls it opaque application data. The generated endpoint has no issuer hook, so ext is always chosen by the caller. Exploiting either half requires an app developer to trust stale or ambiguous docs, and the same doc (authentication.md:713-715) tells them to check privileged scopes against local state. This is contract/doc drift that carries some security risk, not a code defect, so low.

crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/canister_pool/mod.rs:561

Before the first import reset, observe `canister_status` and require an empty module and the exact expected controllers, or require an explicit, separately confirmed 'wipe' flag. Embed a workspace-relative config path or a config digest instead of the absolute path, or remap it before embedding.

infounverifiedhost-icp-network-14 · security · medium confidence
Zeroizing the exported identity PEM is best effort: `Command::output()` reallocation and the trial PEM parsers leave copies of the key that are freed without being zeroed.

Failure scenario

A core dump, swap, or another process on the same host with memory access recovers the operator's private key from freed heap pages after `canic` has 'zeroed' it. The window grows with every query.

Evidence

`run_secret_output` gets stdout through `output_with_executable_busy_retry`, which is `Command::output()` (icp/run.rs:27-43; lib.rs:92-94). That reads with `read_to_end` into a growing Vec, and each reallocation frees the earlier buffer without zeroing it. `exported_active_identity` zeroes only the final Vec (management.rs:211-214). Before that, `parse_exported_identity` tries `BasicIdentity`, then `Secp256k1Identity`, then `Prime256v1Identity::from_pem` (229-240); each decodes PEM and base64 into buffers that are not zeroed. Because of the per-call rebuild in the separate finding above, this repeats for every authenticated query.

Recommendation

Read secret stdout with a preallocated `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` from a piped child instead of `output()`. Parse through `Zeroizing<String>`, detecting the key type from the PEM label so only one parser runs. Combine this with caching the identity for each context.

Cargo.toml:189

Failure scenario

A later change breaks one of these invariants, for example a fixture revision reaching u64::MAX or pool counters being double-counted. The release wasm then wraps and makes admission or bound decisions on corrupted counters instead of trapping and rolling back the message. Debug and test builds (overflow-checks = true) would not show the same behaviour.

`[profile.release] overflow-checks = false` together with `panic = "abort"` (Cargo.toml:182-190). Canister code is almost entirely checked, but a few unchecked operations rely on out-of-band invariants:
- `record.next_chunk += 1; record.received_bytes += len as u64` (crates/canic-control-plane/src/ops/fixture_store/mod.rs:75-76)
- `Self::occupied_asset_capacity() + added_count` and `non_store_asset_count() + pending_creation + pending_imports` (crates/canic-control-plane/src/ops/canister_pool/mod.rs:132, 1276)
- `request.expected_revision + 1` on a Store-observed revision (crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/canister_pool/fixture/mod.rs:61)
- the history reservation arithmetic (crates/canic-core/src/model/public_metrics/history/mod.rs:220-241)

The allocation fold `(reserved + 1, committed)` (crates/canic-control-plane/src/storage/stable/component_registry/mod.rs:3782-3829) is bounded by map size. Each site is currently bounded, but a future invariant break would produce a wrong value rather than a trap.

Recommendation

Enable `overflow-checks = true` for the canister release profile (the instruction cost is negligible next to Canic's validation work). Alternatively, convert the remaining sites to checked_* returning typed errors and add `clippy::arithmetic_side_effects` as a warning on canic-core and canic-control-plane.

Area summaries

Delegated auth: tokens, delegation proofs, signatures, verification

core-auth1 high5 medium7 low

Canic's delegated auth works like this. Root builds a canonical chain-key batch over per-issuer ChainKeyDelegationCertV1 leaves (a Merkle tree with 0x00/0x01 domain separation) and signs the header hash once per batch with management-canister threshold ECDSA. It checks the returned signature locally, then installs issuer-specific DelegationProofs on issuer canisters. Issuers self-issue tokens bound to the caller (presenter == subject == caller), sign the canonical claims hash with an IC canister signature, and use an update-then-query retrieval. Verifiers check everything locally. They pin the configured SEC1 key, key id, derivation hash and key version. They enforce epoch and key-version floors, the policy and batch windows, max_revocation_latency and low-s/zero checks. They check header/leaf/cert coherence, the witness, the issuer DER canister id and seed, and the BLS canister signature against the configured IC root key. Expiry is strict and forward skew is bounded. A heap positive cache is bound to the full proof, claims, issuer proof and caller. Separately, role attestations use root canister signatures, and a local application-session layer turns short-lived tokens into caller-bound sessions with replay tombstones. The cryptographic verification core is careful. I found no way to forge a token or have a proof accepted without verification. Canonical encoding is length-prefixed, domain-separated and strictly validated. Proof-supplied keys are never used as authority. The subject, caller, audience, issuer and root bindings are explicit, and all timestamps are nanoseconds. The main risks are in the root-side renewal and provisioning state machine, not in verification. (1) GetOrCreateDelegationProof reuses in-flight batches only when the caller is a member, and never reuses Installed batches. Any active Component, or lazy repair on an issuer whose template is disabled, can therefore force a new paid sign_with_ecdsa on every call while any template is due. (2) Batch planning has no per-issuer isolation. One bad template (non-canonical grants accepted at upsert) or one issuer policy disabled or narrowed later fails every batch non-retryably. That stops the renewal timer and makes lazy repair fail for all issuers. (3) Any registry-epoch change while no template is due makes the renewal timer stop with an invariant failure. (4) Missing proofs are excluded from lazy repair. Together, (2)-(4) turn routine operator actions into fleet-wide login outages. Smaller issues: the role-attestation side maps on root are never pruned (unbounded heap growth driven by Components), and root signs whatever role-attestation epoch the member asks for, which defeats the epoch floors. The global admission quotas on prepare and sessions can be filled by free principals. The rest are low-severity contract and documentation gaps: the verifier ignores role, the seed-hash binding is never checked, cache hits skip the accept_until window, installs are not monotonic, certified_data ownership is undocumented, and root state access clones the whole state.

Strengths
  • Canonical auth encoding is length-prefixed, per-family domain-separated and rejects non-canonical grant/scope ordering instead of normalizing (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/delegated/canonical.rs:22-39, 222-238, 493-510).
  • Merkle leaves and nodes are domain-separated (0x00 plus a leaf domain vs 0x01), which prevents second-preimage confusion (canonical.rs:247-254; delegated/chain_key.rs:524-530).
  • The root proof verifier pins the configured public key, key id, derivation-path hash and key version. It enforces the epoch and key-version floors, the policy and batch windows, and max_revocation_latency, and it rejects high-s and zero-component ECDSA signatures (delegated/chain_key.rs:161-218, 414-498).
  • Header/leaf/DelegationCert coherence is checked field by field: issuer, algorithm, binding, TTL, audience, grants and window (delegated/chain_key.rs:322-394).
  • Claims binding is strict: presenter == subject == transport caller, strict expiry, bounded forward skew, the token must stay inside the cert window and TTL, and audience and grants must be subsets (delegated/verify.rs:203-290).
  • The positive cache key binds the full proof, claims, issuer proof and caller, and semantic checks still run on every hit (delegated/cache.rs:32-67; token/verification.rs:107-125).
  • Root checks each returned threshold signature locally before persisting it, and stale signing callbacks are discarded by status and header hash (delegated/chain_key_signing.rs:188-198; delegation/chain_key_batch/signing.rs:131-150).
  • Token and role-attestation decoding use bounded candid quotas, attestation proof fields are size-capped, and issuer-local prepare is bounded per caller and globally with caller-bound retrieval (access/auth/token.rs:24-25, 86-95; ops/auth/attestation.rs:172-201; token/retention/mod.rs:69-107).
Not covered

Not read in detail: ops/storage/auth/mapper.rs (only spot-checked), root_issuer_renewal/view.rs, the pure application-authorization policy functions (narrowing, eligibility, admission), model/auth/application_authorization, dto/auth definitions, and the test files (chain_key_batch/tests.rs, token/tests.rs, root_issuer_renewal/tests.rs). I did not audit the internals of the ic-canister-sig-creation SignatureMap (prune bounds, expiry) or ic_signature_verification (DER parsing, certificate delegation checks); I assumed their documented behaviour. The access::auth::authenticated macro path and delegated-session subject replacement belong to neighbouring units. Nothing was executed, per the read-only rules. The instruction-count estimates in the efficiency finding are reasoned, not measured. Cycle costs assume the mainnet key_1 fee of about 26.15B cycles per signature.

Access predicates, API facade, dispatch, ingress, generated endpoints and endpoint macros

core-access-endpoints1 high4 medium8 low

This unit covers the endpoint access layer and the macros that generate endpoints. canic-macros runs parse -> validate -> expand. It requires every endpoint to declare either `public` or `requires(...)`, lowers requires into a single AccessExpr::All, appends a default Fleet-mode guard to non-internal endpoints, and, for `payload(max_bytes)` updates, emits a raw adapter that checks the argument size before decoding (for inter-canister calls as well as ingress). canic-core::access evaluates the builtin predicates: raw-transport caller and topology checks, delegated tokens (the first argument is decoded under a quota), local-subnet role attestations, service authority and Fleet mode. Denials are recorded through record_access_failure. The generated role surfaces (root.rs, role.rs, fleet_coordinator.rs, wasm_store.rs) collapse many commands into one `internal, public` method and authorize each variant inside the handler body. Role-specific inspect_message hooks decode the command and apply per-variant byte limits. Overall the code is deliberate and of high quality. Every root command (43 variants), store command (12) and coordinator command (16) is checked for authorization before any effect. Caller binding uses the raw transport caller throughout. Proof arguments are decoded under explicit quotas, and a mis-selected Fleet-admission evaluator is a terminal failure that neither not() nor any() can invert. I found no forgery or authorization bypass inside the predicates themselves. The main risks lie in what the predicates and surfaces admit, and in how bounds and failures interact: - Delegated tokens can be minted for, and presented by, the anonymous principal, so anonymous callers pass authenticated(cap::VERIFY) guards. - The open token-prepare path shares global replay and retention quotas that Sybil principals can fill, which denies login to everyone. - The root-to-child ConfigureRuntime command is capped at 16 KiB, yet its payload grows with the Fleet directory, Group directory and number of direct children, with no root-side bound. - On Fleet-admission-projection roles, ConfigureRuntime returns an invariant error after it has already committed the directory synchronization. - The inspect_message hooks accept, from any ingress caller including anonymous, variants that only canisters may send, including multi-MiB ProvisionComponents. Root pays the ingress and decode cost before its handler rejects the call. Lower-severity issues: - not() fails open on evaluation errors. - The per-endpoint instruction-accounting stack is shared across interleaved async messages. - Inline per-variant authorization skips the access-denial metrics that the contract requires. - Per-variant authorization uses allow-lists that default to open for new variants. - A guard-suppression heuristic depends on type names (FleetCommand, and FleetStateIs, which exists nowhere). - Fleet-mode gating blinds controller-only observability while the Fleet is Disabled. - The blob deletion queue query is unbounded. - Some authorization and orchestration live below the endpoint layer.

Strengths
  • Explicit access is mandatory: validate() rejects any endpoint without `public` or `requires(...)` and forbids combining them (crates/canic-macros/src/endpoint/validate/mod.rs:70-82). Access-gated endpoints must be async and fallible, so a denial cannot trap (validate/mod.rs:56-68; expand/mod.rs:29-32).
  • not(...) cannot wrap caller::*, auth::* or deployment::* predicates, even when nested (validate/mod.rs:84-89, 156-192). An unselected Fleet-admission evaluator is terminal and cannot be inverted through not/any (access/expr/mod.rs:394, 402, 455-460; test at 705-719).
  • Proof-bearing predicates decode only the first argument, with explicit decoding and type-length quotas, independent of trailing payload size (access/auth/token.rs:24-25, 85-96; access/auth/attestation.rs:18-19, 41-52). The attestation check binds subject == caller, audience == self and the live subnet (ops/auth/verify/mod.rs:30-56).
  • The raw update adapter enforces the declared byte limit before decoding, for inter-canister callers as well as ingress (crates/canic-macros/src/endpoint/expand/mod.rs:364-372), so inspect_message is not relied on as the size boundary.
  • Root, store and coordinator dispatchers authorize every current variant before any effect. Coordinator-only, root-only, parent-only and controller-only variants each get the exact check they need (crates/canic/src/macros/endpoints/root.rs:222-397; wasm_store.rs:80-121; fleet_coordinator.rs:74-110).
  • Retrieval of prepared tokens and attestations is keyed by (hash, prepared_by = msg_caller), so another principal's prepared proof cannot be fetched (crates/canic-core/src/api/auth/token.rs:33-38; workflow/runtime/auth/prepare/mod.rs:241-246).
  • Local application authorization re-reads msg_caller, rejects anonymous callers and callers that differ from the observed caller, and rejects infrastructure principals as session subjects (crates/canic-core/src/access/auth/mod.rs:46-81; access/auth/identity.rs:14-51).
  • Blob gateway endpoints fail closed for non-gateway callers without trapping (crates/canic-core/src/api/blob_storage/gateway.rs:15-37).
Not covered

Not reviewed in depth: - The control-plane authorize_* helpers called from root.rs (root_admission::authorize_coordinator, root_funding::authorize_coordinator, component_registry child/peer allocation authorization, fleet_subnet_root::authorize_root_removal_caller) and the workflows behind ComponentRpcApi, CanisterPoolApi and WasmStore*Api. - The Fleet-activation and authority-restore endpoint fence policies (require_endpoint_for_phase, AuthorityRestoreWorkflow::require_endpoint_allowed). - Delegated-token and attestation cryptographic verification internals, root delegation-proof issuance policy (GetOrCreateDelegationProof) and cascade workflows. - About 700 lines of api/runtime/mod.rs (status rendering) and the full canic-macros parse/validate test suites. - start.rs lifecycle macros, apart from the inspect_message wiring. Could not confirm statically: - The exact encoded sizes behind the 16 KiB ConfigureRuntime finding are estimates from DTO shapes; they were not measured. - Candid zero-sized-element decode bombs: the raw adapter and ic-cdk set only a skipping quota, but I found no command input with a Vec<Option<_>> or all-optional-record shape, so no finding is reported. - The coordinator-to-root ProvisionComponents path permits batches up to 8 MiB + 64 KiB (component_provisioning_plan/mod.rs:60-63), above the IC's 2 MiB cross-subnet message limit. This belongs to control-plane review. No tests or builds were run; everything was traced read-only.

Lifecycle, bootstrap, stable-memory layout, timers, CDK shims, start macros

core-lifecycle-memory4 medium8 low2 info

Canic's lifecycle layer is a two-phase design: the macro-generated `init`/`post_upgrade` exports (crates/canic/src/macros/start.rs) call thin synchronous adapters in crates/canic-core/src/lifecycle. Those adapters set up the shared ic-timers runtime, install the compiled config and role authority, bootstrap the ic-memory manager, restore env/activation state, and trap on any failure. After that the optional synchronous lifecycle participant runs, and async bootstrap and application hooks are deferred to zero-delay `RemoveWhenStopped` timers. Stable storage uses one MemoryManager with fixed IDs whose namespace/range authority is enforced in memory/policy.rs. Records use CBOR through `impl_storable_bounded!`, and singleton cells go through `BoundedCell`. Cross-release upgrades are rejected in post_upgrade through `require_release_build`, which fits the reinstall-only policy. The code quality is high. Ordering is explicit and bootstrap is fail-closed (memory registry before env restore, restore fence before timer start). Memory-ID ownership is checked by prefix and range, record bounds are mostly measured against worst-case encodings, and codegen escapes safely because it uses proc_macro2/quote. The main risks sit where lifecycle meets "same-release restart". The Fleet Coordinator has no post_upgrade at all. An upgrade therefore succeeds and leaves a canister whose every endpoint traps. Post-upgrade restoration overwrites the persisted role instead of checking it. The application install hook is an at-most-once heap timer with no durable retry path. The post-upgrade bootstrap retry has no reclaim path, and a user `init` block gates Canic's own post-upgrade bootstrap. The second group of risks is hot-path cost that grows with fleet or user count and lives in the storage facades. Every managed endpoint deep-clones the 2 MiB activation record and re-hashes the Directory authority twice. Each shard assignment materializes the entire unbounded assignment map. Each root replay admission runs several full scans that fully decode replay receipts. The log query materializes the whole log. Smaller issues are a broken public `canic::perf!` macro, mislabelled fixed-size bounds, and a linear-scan sequence allocator.

Strengths
  • crates/canic-core/src/memory/policy.rs:191-318 enforces stable-key namespace against memory-ID range. canic.core.* and canic.control_plane.* keys are pinned to their ranges, the single-ID infrastructure slots (62-65, 68) are pinned exactly, unknown canic.* namespaces are rejected, and application keys are barred from every reserved range. ic-memory additionally rejects external ic_memory.* keys (ic-memory registry.rs:48).
  • crates/canic-core/src/cdk/bounded_cell/mod.rs validates the complete encoding before the underlying cell writes. It rejects oversize values before any stable effect, and its test proves the memory bytes are unchanged after a rejected write (lines 105-123).
  • Lifecycle ordering is explicit and fail-closed. Root post_upgrade (lifecycle/upgrade/root.rs:19-104) installs config and authority, bootstraps memory, restores env, and restores timer suspension from the durable authority fence before any service starts. Any failure traps, so the upgrade rolls back.
  • Reinstall-only policy is enforced in the actor itself. `FleetActivationOps::require_release_build` (ops/storage/fleet_activation/mod.rs:210-222) makes managed/root post_upgrade reject a module with a different release-build ID, and root upgrades are refused while an ICP refill is resumable (workflow/runtime/mod.rs:152-162).
  • Config and authority codegen (bootstrap/render.rs) renders through proc_macro2 `Literal`/`quote!` instead of string formatting, so escaping is correct. No TOML parser enters wasm: `parse_config_model` and render are `cfg(not(wasm32))`.
  • The init bootstrap retry has a clear typed exhaustion path. `mark_retryable_init_failure_exhausted` plus `try_schedule_nonroot_init` (ops/runtime/bootstrap.rs:102-126) let an exact ConfigureRuntime replay reclaim a transiently failed init bootstrap while collapsing concurrent schedulers.
  • Several stable records have tests asserting exact worst-case encodings (async_job_recovery/mod.rs:133-175; CanisterRecord, IntentRecord bounds), and the log store bounds per-entry message size with UTF-8-safe truncation (storage/stable/log.rs:233-270).
  • The timer authority refuses snapshot sealing while any timer outside Canic custody or any running claim exists (workflow/runtime/timer/mod.rs:471-484), and the durable fence is re-derived into heap suspension on root post_upgrade.
Not covered

I read these only partially: bootstrap/render.rs (skimmed function inventory and escaping approach), storage/stable/intent.rs beyond the record definitions (the receipt eligibility/reservation arithmetic in the second half), storage/stable/auth/records.rs, storage/stable/blob_storage.rs beyond the first ~330 lines, placement_index.rs internals, state_contract.rs beyond the header, and control_plane_support.rs beyond the first 120 lines (re-exports). I did not verify ic-memory 0.14.3 bootstrap internals (ledger recovery, warm-reuse identity checks) or ic-timers 0.8.0 semantics for trapping Once callbacks. Instruction-cost magnitudes in the performance findings are estimates from code structure, not measurements. I did not run any tests or builds (read-only mandate). The control-plane root bootstrap (schedule_post_upgrade_root_bootstrap) and the Coordinator workflow internals were followed only far enough to confirm the lifecycle findings.

Configuration model, validation and generated runtime config

core-config4 medium9 low1 info

Canic configuration is parsed and validated on the host only. `canic::build!` calls `Config::parse_toml` (toml + serde_path_to_error, with deny_unknown_fields everywhere). That step resolves offline chain-key public keys, runs `ConfigModel::validate` and compiles four canonical projections: Component topology, Component Group graph, flattened deployments and Fleet services. Each is length-prefixed, domain-separated and SHA-256 hashed. The build then renders Rust constructor code. Root gets the whole `ConfigModel` plus compacted TOML source. Every other role gets a pruned `RoleRuntimeAuthority` that is installed once at init. No TOML or YAML parser reaches wasm: both parsers are target-gated in canic-core and canic, and toml is only a dev-dependency of canic-control-plane. Cycle amounts are parsed as exact integers with typed overflow and sub-cycle errors. Decoded projections are re-validated against the source graphs. Overall quality is high. Bounds are explicit, arithmetic is checked, canonical ordering is enforced and errors are typed. The main risk is configuration that the build accepts but the runtime rejects or misreads. The most important case: CONFIG.md and the schema tests explicitly allow a descendant role in several Specs, or a Component role that is also a descendant elsewhere. Root's creation plans and root-child funding look roles up by role alone and fail with CONFIGURATION_CONFLICT. Those roles can never be created. Several limits the runtime enforces are not checked at build time: - deployment member-limit reductions below the warm-up count; - initial warm-up trees larger than `maximum_descendants`, or self-recursive ones; - verifier trust anchors (IC root key, chain-key policy) required by non-root init; - per-role attestation epoch floors whose keys are never validated as role names, so a typo silently disables the floor. Secondary issues: CONFIG.md has drifted from the code (K/M cycle units, env var names, a claimed root-key fallback, undocumented grouped-deployment and service sections). Root re-compiles and re-hashes the whole immutable config on every provisioning step. Top-up, log and chain-key fields lack some cross-field and upper-bound checks. No finding reaches critical. Failures are fail-closed and recoverable by fixing the config and reinstalling, but some wedge provisioning for the affected roles or deployment members.

Strengths
  • TOML and serde_path_to_error are target-gated out of the canister wasm graph (crates/canic-core/Cargo.toml `[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies]`; crates/canic-core/src/config/mod.rs:15-16,196-219; crates/canic/Cargo.toml). canic-control-plane has toml only as a dev-dependency.
  • Strict schema: deny_unknown_fields on every struct, with typed unknown-field and invalid-value classification carrying logical paths (crates/canic-core/src/config/mod.rs:128-142,300-329; tests in crates/canic-core/src/bootstrap/mod.rs:288-322).
  • Exact cycle parsing with no floating point, rounding or saturation. It returns typed Overflow, SubcyclePrecision and HumanUnitRequired errors and requires quoted B/T/Q units in config (crates/canic-core/src/cdk/types/cycles.rs:127-351).
  • Canonical, domain-separated, length-prefixed encodings with explicit byte bounds for the topology, group graph and deployment digests (crates/canic-core/src/config/topology/mod.rs:1285-1344; crates/canic-core/src/config/component_deployment_configuration.rs:297-329).
  • Provisioning-grant cycle detection (Kahn's algorithm) runs on the source config and again on decoded or projected topologies (crates/canic-core/src/config/validation/mod.rs:83-153; crates/canic-core/src/config/topology/mod.rs:897-946).
  • Decoded projections are re-validated against the source graphs, including member projections, labels, limits and spec hashes, so stored or decoded state cannot bypass the rules (crates/canic-core/src/config/component_group_deployment/mod.rs:179-208,528-622; member_limit.rs:219-259).
  • The runtime authority is pruned per role and installed exactly once, with a role-match check and topology re-validation (crates/canic-core/src/bootstrap/mod.rs:100-115; crates/canic-core/src/config/runtime.rs:469-488).
  • Build outputs refuse symlinked generated sources, and sums use checked arithmetic throughout (crates/canic/src/build_support/config.rs:76-98; crates/canic-core/src/config/validation/mod.rs:52-58; topology/mod.rs:1029-1033).
Not covered

Read lightly or not at all: - crates/canic-core/src/config/component_group_deployment/canonical.rs and fleet_service/canonical.rs - the large config test files (schema/tests.rs, topology/tests.rs, component_group/tests.rs, component_group_deployment/tests.rs, fleet_service/tests.rs, component_deployment_configuration/tests.rs, ops/config/chain_key/tests.rs), except the targeted tests cited - the ids validators for ComponentSpecId, AppId and the member-path types The host-side config consumers (canic-host release_set/config, fleet_ensure policy) were only checked where needed to confirm or refute a finding. I did not verify whether an undeclared `[roles.wasm_store]` declaration, which validation accepts, affects the host build of the store artifact. Instruction-cost estimates in the efficiency findings are reasoned from the code, not measured. No builds or tests were run, so none of the findings has a reproducing test yet.

Role contracts, replay policy, intent journal, async job recovery, authority restore

core-intent-replay1 critical1 medium7 low

This unit covers Canic's durable reservation and replay primitives. The local intent store (`ops/storage/intent`) keeps expirable reservations: primary records, a pending index, a finite-expiry index, per-resource totals and aggregate metadata. The cost guard uses it for per-window quota and cycle reservations. The receipt-backed store keeps exact-key reservations addressed by OperationId. Application receipts carry a replay deadline and a terminal-eligibility index used for bounded reclamation. Canic-owned placement receipts carry an acknowledgement index. The shared replay receipt store (`ops/replay`) gates root capabilities and other protected commands. Receipts go Reserved -> ExternalEffectInFlight -> staged -> Committed, or RecoveryRequired, and are keyed by (command_kind, operation_id). The async-job fence (`ops/storage/async_job_recovery`) gives each recovery-critical owner a serial lease with takeover after expiry. For cycle top-up it also keeps a stable operation generation. The authority-restore fence seals root/coordinator mutation around snapshot capture and reopens only when live IC history still matches the seal. Mechanically the code is careful. Every mutation validates first and applies second, with no await in between. Indexes are cross-checked against primaries, counters use checked arithmetic, typed errors are mapped explicitly, and stale async completions cannot clear a successor lease. The fence and role-contract resolution are small, pure and well tested. The main risks come from lifetime and retention policy, not from the mechanics: - **Resource totals (critical):** committed totals are never reclaimed, yet the 0.96.7 cap of 1,000 resource-total identities is shared with cost-guard quota keys that include a 60-second time bucket. After about 1,000 active quota minutes, every cost-guarded operation on root (child cycles funding, provisioning, ICP refill, publication) fails permanently. - **Replay TTL (high):** receipt expiry is fixed at reservation + TTL (at most 300 s). Expired Committed receipts are purged. A same-ID retry after purge is admitted as Fresh, so the "exact retry identity" only dedups inside that window. Cycle top-up takeover fires only after a 5-minute lease, i.e. after the TTL. - **Replay namespace (medium):** the slot key is not actor-scoped, while placement and top-up operation IDs are publicly derivable. One fleet member can pre-occupy another's operation IDs. - **Growth and capacity (medium):** local intent records are never deleted. The 1,000-record receipt store is shared between application receipts (held at least 15 minutes after settlement) and Canic placement receipts.

Strengths
  • Validate-then-apply discipline across the intent store: `try_reserve`, `commit_at`, `abort`, `settle_pair_at` (crates/canic-core/src/ops/storage/intent/mod.rs:400-878) finish every check and compute the new totals before touching storage. The two-intent cost settlement is atomic within one message.
  • Receipt-backed begin/settle is exact-key and CAS-based: `retained_begin_result` rejects payload, resource, quantity or deadline drift as BindingConflict. `settle_if_pending` enforces the expected revision and exact terminal-evidence equality, and returns an error on contradictory evidence instead of overwriting (ops/storage/intent/mod.rs:1062-1150, 1487-1525).
  • Resource namespace ownership is enforced both in the store (`validate_receipt_admission_owner`, :1636-1659) and in the workflow (`ensure_consumer_resource_key` / `ensure_canic_owned_resource_key`, workflow/runtime/intent.rs:288-318), so application code cannot settle or observe `canic:` reservations.
  • Replay tokens carry the full receipt identity and every mutation re-checks it (`latest_receipt_for_token` / `same_receipt_identity`, ops/replay/receipt.rs:493-519). In-flight and recovery receipts survive expiry and purge (storage/stable/replay.rs:413-418), so an uncertain effect is never forgotten.
  • The async-job fence cannot be cleared by a stale completion (`finish_attempt` / `finish_replay_safe_attempt` require the exact generation). Cycle top-up keeps its operation generation across takeover and retryable failure (ops/storage/async_job_recovery/mod.rs:303-368).
  • The authority-restore fence fails closed. Prepare suspends timers and seals, trapping on any post-await failure so the suspension rolls back. Resume requires the exact operation ID and an unchanged IC history count, which by design keeps a restored snapshot sealed (ops/storage/authority_restore/mod.rs:95-155; workflow/runtime/authority_restore.rs:128-172).
  • Application terminal-eligibility capacity is pre-reserved in stable memory before admission (`reserve_application_eligibility_capacity`, storage/stable/intent.rs), so settlement can never fail for lack of pages after the external effect.
  • Role-contract resolution is pure and deterministic. It rejects missing required features and surplus crypto features, and detects memory-ID collisions during allocation materialization (role_contract/policy.rs:26-104, 319-347).
Not covered

Only skimmed or not read: - role_contract/model.rs, profile.rs and tests.rs. - The full role_contract catalog: allocation tables were checked only for structure, not audited row by row against the storage actually used at runtime. - replay_policy/endpoint_manifest.rs, most of role_command_manifest.rs and the replay_policy tests. - The stable encodings for authority_restore and async_job_recovery records. - Most of ops/storage/intent/tests.rs, async_job_recovery/tests.rs and authority_restore/tests.rs. Not assessed: - Whether ic-timers watchdog timing guarantees hold. - The control-plane component lifecycle that consumes the root provision operation ID. - The IcpRefill domain store's own reconciliation, where `abort_uncommitted_receipt` is used. Instruction-count estimates for the replay-store scans are reasoned from the code, not measured. No code was executed.

Inter-canister RPC, management-canister calls, cascade, cost guard, ICRC, infra

core-rpc-ic1 high3 medium5 low1 info

This unit covers the IC call wrappers (infra::ic::call, ops::ic::call, the public api::call builder), management-canister adapters (deposit, install, uninstall, stop, delete, status, history, settings, ECDSA), root-capability RPC (envelope and freshness checks, structural proof, replay-first handlers for provision, recycle and cycles funding), ICP-to-cycles refill (ICP ledger transfer followed by CMC notify_top_up), Cycles Ledger adapters, and state/topology cascades. Every value-moving management or ledger call in these paths uses unbounded wait. Paid effects are journalled before they happen: the replay receipt is marked ExternalEffectInFlight together with its cost-guard settlement ids before the await. ICP refill is designed carefully: ledger deduplication uses a fixed created_at_time and memo, a Duplicate reply is handled, and policy is re-checked after every await. Engineering quality is high, but one recovery gap is serious. When a parent's deposit_cycles to a child fails, the handler marks the child-funding receipt RecoveryRequired{ExternalEffectStatusUnknown}. That receipt survives expiry forever, counts as pending, and has no code that resumes or clears it. The same handler also restores the funding ledger and releases the cycle reservation, so the code treats the transfer as not having happened, yet the receipt then blocks every later funding request from that child. A likely trigger is ordinary: the preflight checks the native balance, while ic-cdk checks the liquid balance before sending. A parent close to its freezing reserve can therefore permanently lose the ability to fund a child. The child's retry logic makes things worse. A remote typed rejection is always retried (observed_public sets PLATFORM_FAILED), but a local transport reject or a liquid-balance shortfall is terminal. The child therefore loops forever on the wedge, or its automatic top-up stops after a transient reject. Other risks: cycles attached to bounded-wait calls (Coordinator to Root AcceptFunding, Cashier top-up) can be burned when the reply is SYS_UNKNOWN, and the call builder does not guard against it. ICP refill turns final after 5 notify attempts, including attempts spent before any CMC call, which leaves transferred ICP at the CMC. Smaller issues: replay-store full scans on every root-capability request, a 16 KiB inter-canister payload ceiling that the create-canister sender never checks, heap-held call metrics with no size bound, the replay TTL equalling the child job lease (a possible double grant when a retry comes after expiry), and sequential nested cascade fan-out.

Strengths
  • All value-moving management and ledger calls in scope use unbounded wait, so a rejection is definitive: deposit_cycles (crates/canic-core/src/infra/ic/mgmt/cycles.rs:43), install/uninstall/stop/delete (infra/ic/mgmt/lifecycle.rs:92-193), ICP ledger/CMC (infra/ic/icp_refill.rs:313-371), Cycles Ledger (infra/ic/cycles_ledger.rs:180-251).
  • Intent is recorded before the effect: the replay receipt is set to ExternalEffectInFlight with its cost-guard settlement ids before the deposit await (workflow/rpc/request/handler/nonroot_cycles.rs:418-424; ops/replay/receipt.rs:384-397), and receipt tokens are checked for exact identity before every mutation (ops/replay/receipt.rs:495-518).
  • A concurrent funding operation for the same child is rejected while another is pending, so the ledger snapshot restored after an await cannot overwrite a concurrent grant (nonroot_cycles.rs:382-410).
  • ICP refill reuses a fixed created_at_time and memo so the ledger deduplicates retries, maps Duplicate to the original block (workflow/ic/icp_refill/execution.rs:365-382), treats unknown-effect receipts as resumable (workflow/ic/icp_refill/replay.rs:79-86), and re-validates policy and its hash after every await (workflow/ic/icp_refill/mod.rs:278-292).
  • Capability metadata freshness uses checked arithmetic and bounded clock skew (workflow/rpc/capability/replay.rs:21-54). Structural proof binds the caller, parent and target exactly (workflow/rpc/capability/proof.rs:17-78).
  • The state cascade refuses to forward an obsolete snapshot after an await (workflow/cascade/state.rs:141-148) and validates and bounds each child report (ops/cascade_report/mod.rs:25, 64-113). Topology snapshots are structurally validated before they are applied (ops/cascade.rs:190-289).
  • Mainnet ICP ledger/CMC overrides are refused unless explicitly allowed (infra/ic/icp_refill.rs:292-309). Nat values are converted to u64/u128 with checks everywhere (infra/ic/cycles_ledger.rs:254-264, infra/ic/icp_refill.rs:285-289, infra/ic/mgmt/cycles.rs:50-55).
Not covered

Not reviewed in depth: control-plane Component Registry lifecycle (reserve_child_allocation, subtree removal) behind RootCapabilityLifecycleExecutor; the Fleet Coordinator funding journal and its reconcile path (only the bounded-wait call site was read); blob-storage Cashier workflows beyond the top-up call; auth prepare replay families that share the replay store (whether they can exhaust the global cap of 10,000 root-capability receipts); stable replay storage internals beyond the scan and expiry helpers; and endpoint-macro auth gates for RootCommand/CanisterCommand beyond the dispatch arms I read. The IC best-effort refund semantics behind the bounded-wait finding come from protocol knowledge and were not verified in this repo or against the spec. No code was executed, so no finding is reproduced.

Runtime env, metrics, public metrics, funding usage, runtime workflows

core-runtime-metrics2 medium7 low

This unit covers four things. The first is Canic's protected metrics tables: heap thread-locals in ops/runtime/metrics/*, projected to the controller-only `canic_observability Metrics`. The second is the optional public metrics pipeline: one 5-minute ic-timers task (workflow/metrics/publication/timer) samples the selected families into a heap snapshot cache and a 288-slot heap history (model/public_metrics), and the anonymous `canic_public_status` query only projects that cache. The third is the runtime log: the `log!` macro, LogRetentionWorkflow and a count-bounded stable BTreeMap. The fourth is endpoint/checkpoint instruction instrumentation (perf.rs), plus funding-usage observation, recent-failure and bootstrap diagnostics, and the runtime start/timer-custody workflows. Overall quality is high. Public reads are cache-only. Sampling reads bounded prefixes and rejects oversized labels before cloning. Replacements are validated atomically and keep the previous snapshot on rejection. History byte accounting is conservative, and counter deltas are strict. Funding usage reports missing evidence as unknown, not zero. Timer custody has rollback, and suspension cancels exact claims. Counters saturate throughout. The main defects are correctness and robustness gaps where the aggregation dimensions don't match storage keys, and where untrusted activity shares bounded operator resources: - ICP-refill status counts are keyed per automatic sequence and error code, but the projection drops both. That produces duplicate rows, so the root `operations` public family is rejected permanently once a second automatic refill completes. - Any anonymous caller can flush the count-bounded runtime log, because access denials on update endpoints commit Warn entries. - The Root observability relay is blocked while the Fleet is Readonly. - Endpoint and checkpoint instruction accounting uses canister-global state across interleaved call contexts. - Lower-impact issues: - Full materialization of paged collections: logs, cycle history, public children. - `log!` hot-path cost. - Unvalidated `max_age_secs`, which can block runtime start. - Unbounded inter-canister call metric keys. - Per-principal funding rows in the public `operations` family. - A sticky global history `truncated` flag. No critical or high issues were found in these paths. Nothing here moves cycles or changes authorization directly.

Strengths
  • Public queries only project cached data and never sample, call or mutate. History reads filter expired slots without mutating the cache (crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/public_metrics/mod.rs:90-226; crates/canic-core/src/model/public_metrics/history/mod.rs:342-361).
  • Sampling reads bounded ordered prefixes per owner and validates full series-name length before allocating (crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/metrics/mod.rs:76-113; crates/canic-core/src/perf.rs:220-247; crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/public_metrics/mod.rs:341-350). Enum-keyed process owners reject oversized tables before scanning (crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/public_metrics/process/mod.rs:19-66).
  • Snapshot replacement is atomic and validated. It rejects empty or oversize text, future timestamps, duplicate series and regressed source times, and keeps the previous snapshot with its original sample time (crates/canic-core/src/model/public_metrics/mod.rs:60-128).
  • History storage uses fixed 288-slot groups with conservative byte accounting that includes vacant positions, a series cap and group release on expiry. Counter deltas require adjacent slots, the same window, no saturation and increasing time (crates/canic-core/src/model/public_metrics/history/mod.rs:192-292, 379-392; crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/public_metrics/mod.rs:300-328).
  • Funding-usage observation is read-only and reports missing or mismatched reservation evidence as None (unknown) rather than zero (crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/funding_usage/mod.rs:25-80).
  • The recent-failure ring is heap-only, capped at 16 entries, strips control characters and truncates at byte limits on UTF-8 boundaries (crates/canic-core/src/ops/runtime/recent_failure.rs:10-122).
  • Timer custody rolls back the registration if retention fails. Authority suspension checks every live claim is Canic-owned and not running before cancelling exact claims (crates/canic-core/src/workflow/runtime/timer/mod.rs:131-187, 422-460).
  • Log retention uses exact age deadlines with 256-entry batches and ContinueImmediately for due backlogs, and deadline overflow fails closed (crates/canic-core/src/workflow/runtime/log.rs:103-175).
Not covered

Only skimmed or not reviewed in depth: workflow/runtime/auth/* (renewal, prepare, provisioning, root_issuer, root_delegation_batch); workflow/runtime/fleet_activation.rs; most of workflow/runtime/intent.rs; the cycle top-up state machine in workflow/runtime/cycles/mod.rs; ops/runtime/metrics/{delegated_auth,root_capability,scaling,sharding,cascade,replay,management_call,system,auth/*}.rs beyond their key and cardinality shape; ops/runtime/metrics/tests.rs and the public-metrics memory tests.
