  • Paged Root pool inventory is authority-consistent: config, pending creation and lifecycle counts must match across pages and reconcile with declared totals (EstatePoolInventoryAccumulator 271-368).
  • Status responses are bound to the requested identity, and the public non-controller projection is rejected (1763-1769, 5548-5562); a versionless ICP status falls back to a typed management status call for install version proof (5152-5180).
  • Protocol artifacts are hash-verified and size-bounded before use, and template rendering rejects unresolved bindings and malformed operation identities (protocol.rs:299-335, 380-421).
  • Native funding completion requires a Ledger receipt and a burn-aware lower bound while tolerating donations (native_funding_applied 5280-5328).
  • Batched reads are drained, then consumed in configured order, so an earlier failure keeps precedence and no later batch starts (1188-1211, 3063-3104, 2275-2312).
Not covered

I could not verify icp-cli behaviour for `canister settings update --remove-all-controllers --add-controller` (whether it is one atomic update_settings call) or `canister install` file handling, because icp-cli is not vendored. Cycles Ledger deduplication semantics after FailedToCreate/FailedToWithdraw are inferred, not read from source. Modules this adapter calls were not reviewed in depth: current_protocol, authority_seal, install_history, current_inventory, canic_init, independent_effects, infrastructure_bootstrap and bounded_observations. From tests.rs (8.5k lines) I only sampled the funding and lost-reply tests. I did not assess ic-agent query-signature verification settings, or cached subnet-catalog freshness used for subnet bindings.

Release sets, policy gate, evidence envelopes, build provenance, fleet packages, metadata, state manifest

host-release-set2 medium11 low1 info

This unit covers the host-side trust chain from a build to a deployable release. Each complete `canic build` compiles three child manifests under `.canic/release-builds/<id>/`: the application artifact union, the infrastructure artifact manifest and the fixture artifact manifest. Their SHA-256 digests are bound into one `current-release-set-manifest.json`, and that file's digest is then recorded when the release-build plan is finalized. Every persisted document is written with create-new semantics, re-read through no-follow regular-file readers and rejected unless it re-serializes to identical canonical JSON. Artifact evidence is computed from the actual bytes: gzip is decoded under a bound and compared with the raw Wasm, and the raw Wasm must embed the release-build identity. Root projections (`FleetSubnetRootReleaseSetManifest`) re-derive the exact per-root closure and are checked against the runtime DTO encoding. The policy gate, evidence envelope and build-provenance modules form a separate CI evidence path that is passive and informational. The state manifest is a diagnostic audit of declared memory domains. `fleet_package` generates the Cargo packages for the Root, Coordinator and Store infrastructure canisters. The core release-set integrity code is careful. I found no path traversal, no hash-binding gap and no TOCTOU defect between verification and use in `release_set/`. Consumers re-verify artifact bytes against the recorded size and hash before Store publication, and the root re-derives the manifest digest from canonical bytes. The remaining release-set risks are architectural. The digest chain from finalized plan to current manifest to child manifests is re-implemented by each consumer rather than owned by `release_set`, and several consumers bind only part of it. The application build "targets" are built from the build outputs, so the target-versus-output checks can never fail. An orphaned, uncompiled `manifest.rs` still sits in the tree. The more concrete defects are outside the artifact chain. Workspace state-manifest resolution merges roles across Apps by bare role name. Two Apps whose Root (or a shared role name) resolves to different contracts are reported as "multiple Cargo packages", which blocks `canic state audit`, `canic state manifest` and `canic medic` in multi-App workspaces, including this repository's `apps/demo` plus `apps/test`. Evidence envelopes carry a `payload_sha256` that nothing verifies, while `canic evidence compare` ignores the payload body and relies on that field. The digest also covers `generated_at`, so two envelopes for the same artifact never compare as equal. Build-provenance fields misreport Cargo features, and the clean-source determination can be hidden by git configuration. The generated infrastructure packages seed their own `Cargo.lock` once and never re-sync it, so the most privileged canisters can keep stale transitive dependencies after a workspace `cargo update`.

Strengths
  • Canonical-bytes discipline on every retained document: parse, re-serialize and require byte equality before accepting (crates/canic-host/src/release_set/application/persistence/mod.rs:403-412, infrastructure/persistence/mod.rs:434-442, current/mod.rs:249-253, fixture/persistence/mod.rs:127-131).
  • Immutable create-new publication with lost-response and competing-writer reconciliation, and finalized builds refuse to acquire or repair evidence (application/persistence/mod.rs:177-214, infrastructure/persistence/mod.rs:214-255, fixture/persistence/mod.rs:203-226).
  • Artifact evidence is derived from bytes, never from caller hashes: the gzip is decoded with a bounded `take(size+1)` and compared with the raw Wasm, magic bytes are checked, and the raw Wasm must embed the release-build identity (release_set/application/mod.rs:831-879, infrastructure/mod.rs:306-354, application/persistence/mod.rs:254-263).
  • Filesystem containment: artifact reads canonicalize the parent under the canonical root and read the final component no-follow, and fixture reads reject a symlink at every path component (release_set/artifact/mod.rs:59-110, fixture/persistence/mod.rs:172-201).
  • Host and runtime root-manifest encodings are tested for byte parity, and the root independently re-derives canonical bytes and digest before trusting a manifest (release_set/application/tests.rs:414,726; canic-control-plane/src/workflow/bootstrap/root_store/mod.rs:160-169).
  • Fixture inputs are hash-bound before the build and re-verified before finalization (`verify_unchanged`, `verify_retained`), and every retained chunk is re-verified against its descriptor on read (release_set/fixture/configuration/mod.rs:35-58, fixture/persistence/mod.rs:157-170).
  • Policy TOML uses `deny_unknown_fields`, a custom strict deserializer for build-provenance rules and non-empty validation of allow-lists and rules (policy_gate/model/mod.rs:30-132, policy_gate/validation/mod.rs:7-44).
  • Config mutations re-parse the edited source before writing, and a role rename rolls the config back if the package-manifest write fails (release_set/config/mutation/rename.rs:69-73, release_set/config/mod.rs:293-325).
Not covered

Not reviewed in depth: canister_build (the artifact finalizer, build reuse and input snapshots) and release_build (the plan state machine). I read these only where they bind to release-set evidence. The fleet_ensure consumers were checked only to confirm how they bind digests and verify artifact bytes before Store publication. The detailed fixture tests, release_set/tests/*, release_set/config/error.rs and config/projection/* were only skimmed. canic_metadata was reviewed for binding logic only; the query is uncertified and used for reporting. Nothing was executed, per the read-only rules, so the claims about Cargo lockfile behaviour under `cargo metadata` without `--locked`, git's `status.showUntrackedFiles` handling and the multi-App state-audit failure are reasoned from code and documented tool behaviour, not reproduced. Windows-specific path behaviour was not assessed; the durable_io readers are unix-only.

Canister builds, release builds, toolchain, ic-wasm and binaryen, artifact IO, cargo metadata, candid endpoints

host-canister-build4 medium7 low1 info

This unit turns an App config into finalized Wasm artifacts. The CLI (crates/canic-cli/src/build.rs) resolves a context, preflights one exact ic-wasm and, for release builds, one checksum-pinned Binaryen (build_toolchain, ic_wasm, binaryen). It then either returns a verified complete-build cache hit (canister_build/reuse) or plans a fresh nonce-derived release identity (release_build), builds it and seals it. canister_build/artifact.rs compiles the Coordinator and Store from generated packages and captures their bytes right away. It then partitions configured roles into feature-compatible Cargo batches per workspace, runs a no-LTO declaration pass, extracts Candid (with a byte-keyed extraction cache), derives protocol digests, runs the runtime pass and finalizes every role in parallel. artifact_io stages shrink, Candid metadata, wasm-opt -Oz with contract-parity checks, the code-limit check and deterministic gzip, and publishes only after qualification. Overall quality is high. Tool admission is strict for Binaryen. The staging and qualification pipeline, the canonical CBOR release plans, the environment normalization and the post-build input revalidation are careful, and most of it is well tested. Production code has almost no panics, and the Wasm parser is bounded. The main risks sit at the edges where Cargo's model and Canic's assumptions diverge: - Every workspace shares one target directory, and artifacts are located by package-name convention rather than by what Cargo reports. Same-named packages from different workspaces overwrite each other. A custom `[lib] name` gives a missing or stale file. - Build-mode role validation resolves dependencies without `--locked`, so the `--locked` on the actual build is vacuous and the user's Cargo.lock can be rewritten. - The generated infrastructure Cargo.lock is copied from the workspace lock once and then drifts. - The complete-build cache key covers only the context workspace. Manifests and lockfiles of other role workspaces and of the generated workspaces are outside it, so their changes can produce stale hits. - Configured-role finalization is not bounded, so large fleets can exhaust memory running concurrent wasm-opt processes. - Smaller gaps: normal builds never check exports against Candid; implicit sccache overrides a config-level rustc wrapper; paths are not remapped, which weakens cross-machine determinism; `canic endpoints` expands Candid types exponentially.

Strengths
  • Binaryen admission pins both the archive SHA-256 and the platform executable SHA-256 before running it, then re-admits the staged copy before an atomic rename plus directory fsync (crates/canic-host/src/binaryen/mod.rs:348-395, 470-542).
  • Finalization stages every candidate in a private directory, cleans it up in Drop, and publishes only after shrink, metadata, optimizer, code-limit and sidecar checks have all passed (crates/canic-host/src/artifact_io/mod.rs:67-139, 141-208).
  • The release optimizer proves export-inventory, embedded public-Candid and feature-set parity before it replaces the input, and it records before/after metrics plus the tool digest (crates/canic-host/src/artifact_io/mod.rs:454-602).
  • Release-build plans use canonical CBOR with nonce-derived identity. Finalization is one-way, runs under an flock and re-reads after a write error, and decode rejects non-canonical bytes (crates/canic-host/src/release_build/mod.rs:286-329, 393-458).
  • A single build_environment module drives both child-process environments and cache fingerprints, so withheld keys and the SHLVL value cannot drift apart (crates/canic-host/src/build_environment/mod.rs:14-44).
  • The Candid extraction cache is keyed by exact Wasm bytes, the extractor hash, the implementation and the environment. After extracting it re-verifies the extractor and the Wasm, and it degrades to ordinary extraction on any cache fault (crates/canic-host/src/canister_build/candid_cache/mod.rs:113-209).
  • Post-build input validation rechecks inputs that dropped out of the inventory and rejects inputs first seen after compilation, writing bounded, value-free rejection evidence (crates/canic-host/src/canister_build/reuse/snapshot/mod.rs:37-109, reuse/diagnostics/rejection/mod.rs:108-154).
  • The Wasm section parser is bounds-checked: LEB128 overflow guards, rejection of truncated sections and duplicate code/data/export/function sections, and function/code count consistency (crates/canic-host/src/artifact_io/wasm/mod.rs:234-435).
Not covered

These files were not read in depth: reuse/lock/inspection and serialization (Linux /proc lock diagnostics), build_provenance, release_set (manifest construction and verification), most test modules, the candid_endpoints tests, and the full role_contract package validation logic. External tool semantics were not executed. In particular, it is unverified whether `wasm-opt --print-features` reports enabled or used features (the feature-parity check may be vacuous), whether the macOS Binaryen archive's wasm-opt needs a sibling dylib, and exactly how Cargo re-uplifts outputs of fresh units. Whether the canister runtime rejects a Wasm compiled for another role at install time was not traced. That bears on the downstream impact of finding 1. No commands were run, per the read-only rules. The exact IC code-section and custom-section limits were not independently confirmed.

ICP CLI integration, network selection, replica queries, subnet catalog, local fleet, durable IO, entropy, discovery

host-icp-network2 medium11 low1 info

This unit is the host side of Canic's link to the ICP CLI and the network. `IcpCli` builds `icp` subprocess commands. It pins the working directory with `--project-root-override`, the identity with `--identity` and an optional password file, and the target with `-e <env>` or, for a direct local replica, `-n url -k root_key`. It checks the CLI version and handles secret export output separately from ordinary output. Typed management updates and read-only queries go through `ic-agent`. The agent's URL and root key come from `icp network status`, and the key comes from `icp identity export`, checked against `icp identity principal`. The `network` module enrolls a DER root trust anchor for each non-mainnet environment. `icp_config` reads `icp.yaml` with serde-saphyr (host-only, capped at 1 MiB, strict options) and classifies each environment as Ic or Local. `durable_io` publishes files atomically: a sibling temp file is written and synced, then renamed or linked into place with no-replace, then the directory is synced; reads refuse to follow a final symlink. `local_fleet` wraps a PocketIC instance. It retains intent before each effect, uses exact-session reset records and a Cycles Ledger `created_at_time` to reconcile lost replies. Overall quality is high. Typed errors, bounded reads, exact-session checks and intent-before-effect records are consistent throughout. The main risks come from two network classifications that can disagree. `icp.yaml` treats every environment that is not `ic` as Local. The canonical network ID is derived from whatever root key was enrolled. Nothing stops an operator enrolling the mainnet root key under a Local environment. The result is a mainnet deployment built as a local build, which enables endpoints gated `build_local_only`. The same Local classification sends readiness queries for any non-`ic` environment to `127.0.0.1` on the port of the `local` network. That includes custom managed networks, remote connected networks and the local-fleet harness gateway, so `canic list` and `canic status` report the wrong network. On durability, a process killed mid-write (Ctrl-C terminates without unwinding) leaves a `.<name>.canic-tmp-*` staging file in the destination directory. Nothing ever removes it. Readers that list directories, such as the capacity-import history scan, then fail to decode it, and same-release recovery cannot finish until someone deletes the file by hand. On Apple platforms the directory sync is a plain fsync, not F_FULLFSYNC. Smaller issues: - Every authenticated query or status call re-exports the private key and spawns 2–4 `icp` processes. The docs call this deliberate, but it costs around a second per call. - Two tracked source files are never compiled and describe code that does not exist. - The raw replica HTTP client has no timeouts. - Some ICP CLI JSON shapes use `deny_unknown_fields`, although the supported range is any 1.x release.

Strengths
  • crates/canic-host/src/durable_io/mod.rs:421-512 atomically publishes each file. It writes a sibling temp with O_EXCL, syncs it, renames with no-replace and falls back to `linkat`, syncs the parent directory, and fsyncs every created ancestor. Reads open with O_NOFOLLOW/O_NONBLOCK and check the file type with fstat, which closes the lstat-to-open race (374-407).
  • crates/canic-host/src/icp/management.rs:203-226 checks the exported PEM's Principal against `icp identity principal`. This catches a default identity changing between lookup and export. `bind_selected_identity` (icp/identity.rs:12-18) freezes the identity for the operation and for every clone of its transport.
  • crates/canic-host/src/icp/query/mod.rs:171-199 retries only typed transient failures (408/429/502-504, connect or timeout errors), with per-attempt and overall deadlines. Signature, certificate, size and decode failures are never retried, and the response body is capped at 8 MiB.
  • crates/canic-host/src/icp_config/manifest/mod.rs:118-169 parses YAML with merge keys rejected, unsupported tags rejected, strict booleans and a 1 MiB cap. It refuses a redeclared `ic` network, external manifest paths and dependency graphs. serde-saphyr is a dependency of canic-host only.
  • crates/canic-host/src/local_fleet: allocation intent (ops/mod.rs:166-207) is recorded before the Ledger call and reconciled through `created_at_time` and `Duplicate` (ops/runtime/mod.rs:89-144). Reset is bound to an exact session with interruption and terminal-replay records (ops/reset/mod.rs:26-86). Each generation gets its own `instance-<session>` directory, so a late orphan write cannot reach a new instance.
  • crates/canic-host/src/network/mod.rs:171-259 enrolls in a crash-resumable order: root key, then enrollment record, then profile. It verifies the fingerprint before writing anything and rejects contradictory partial authority (332-394).
  • crates/canic-host/src/icp/run.rs:27-43 keeps secret CLI output away from String conversion and from error diagnostics, and zeroes stdout when the command fails.
  • crates/canic-host/src/subnet_catalog/acquisition/mod.rs:91-132 gives catalog acquisition one overall deadline with typed progress. A timeout never falls back to weaker cached evidence.
Not covered

Read partially or not at all: icp_config/tests.rs, subnet_catalog/tests/**, diagnostics/generated/mod.rs (generated catalog), local_fleet/tests.rs, the canonical_root and bootstrap_* tests, format/tests.rs, most of icp/tests.rs and icp/query/tests.rs, and examples/local_fleet.rs. Not assessed: how ic-query agrees and certifies the Subnet Catalog; ic-agent query-signature internals; PocketIC and ic_testkit behaviour, such as whether state directories can contain symlinks or grow past 100k entries; exact `icp` CLI 1.5/1.6 JSON output and whether it allows a connected network aimed at mainnet (assumed yes; not verified against icp-cli source); interplay between bootstrap_* builds and the build cache (the build unit owns that); Windows code paths. Downstream consequences in fleet_ensure, canic-cli and canic-control-plane were followed only far enough to confirm or refute findings in this unit.

Host role contracts, protocol binding, canister protocol, component operation and topology, observatory, frontend

host-contract-topology1 high2 medium4 low1 info

This unit covers the host-side code that turns retained Fleet evidence into typed calls and exports. role_contract validates Cargo packages: one direct `canic` edge, no protected-package paths outside it, one ic-memory identity, the feature closure checked against the catalogue, and exactly one `canic::build!`. protocol_binding admits a Candid sidecar before transport only when its SHA-256 and protocol-profile digest reproduce the retained registry binding. canister_protocol wraps icp CLI calls, and its inspection preflight reads the bound Candid contract. component_operation implements `canic component plan/apply/status`. It keeps one hash-sealed local record, reserves the record before submitting, keeps the same operation ID for replay, checks that progress only moves forward, and takes both the Ensure lock and a per-record lock. component_topology finalizes Root admissions against the core topology validators. The observatory makes bounded, query-only collections and produces a curated, escaped public projection, and it compares saved cost reports. frontend exports a digest-sealed browser bundle, checks native cycle capacity, and reads uploaded assets back through queries. Code quality is high. Everything fails closed, errors are typed, sizes are bounded, and file I/O goes through durable no-follow helpers. The paths also follow the documented contracts closely. The main risks come from how the pieces connect, not from local slips. (1) A component operation binds the SHA-256 of the whole Coordinator FleetRegistry. That registry is republished on every admission change, so an ordinary `canic admission apply` blocks every existing and in-flight component operation. (2) Component operations, the observatory and the frontend export still read Candid from the mutable `.icp/<env>/canisters` build directory. Admission and terminal inventory were moved to the immutable selected release for the same reason (tracked as CANIC-108). (3) The saved-report comparison uses the live `ic0.canister_version` as its window anchor. The IC increments that value on every executed message, so real comparisons are always rejected. (4) Component completion and the new canister Principal are accepted from a single uncertified query and kept permanently. The remaining findings are low severity: an ambiguous mapping of STATE_UNAVAILABLE to "absent", a successful update reported as a failure when temp-file cleanup fails, and frontend admission-origin checks that use stale retained admission data. No finding in this unit allows cycle theft or canister takeover. The Root's own operation-ID deduplication and caller checks, which I confirmed in canic-control-plane, prevent a replay from creating a second allocation.

Strengths
  • component_operation/workflow/mod.rs:56-110 persists the reservation (`ops::reserve`) before `transport.submit` and always resubmits the same random operation_id. The Root deduplicates by operation_id and origin (canic-control-plane workflow/component_registry/mod.rs:713-726), so a lost response cannot allocate a second identity.
  • component_operation/policy/mod.rs:18-93 builds live authority as a named `AuthorityBinding` struct that deliberately leaves out `source_plan_sha256`. This follows the AGENTS.md guidance on grouping authority equality. validate_progress (96-151) ties progress to the derived ComponentInstanceId and keeps phase and completion monotonic.
  • protocol_binding/mod.rs:181-227 recomputes both the Candid SHA-256 and the protocol-profile digest from no-follow bytes before any transport. The release variant (release/mod.rs:53-121) also checks manifest digests and sidecar containment.
  • role_contract/package/mod.rs:850-902 and 1331-1429 compare the Canic features actually enabled in the package-selected `cargo tree --no-dedupe` against the canonical closure. They reject protected-package paths outside the direct Canic subtree and reject multiple ic-memory identities, which prevents drift from feature unification.
  • observatory/ops/presentation/mod.rs escapes all rendered text (including the embedded JSON) and uses a finite LimitedWriter, a no-store policy and a restrictive CSP. public_view drops Principals, hashes, placement and funding, and the process runner (ops/transport/process/mod.rs) bounds both output streams and kills and reaps only its own child.
  • frontend/ops/bundle/mod.rs publishes through atomic create-new staging and writes the manifest last. safe_file rejects traversal and symlinks at every path component. verify_bundle requires an independently retained digest and re-hashes every listed file.
  • observatory/policy/cost/mod.rs grant_adjusted_decrease cancels opposing terms before adding them, so exact u128 arithmetic cannot overflow part-way, and zero never gets a negative sign.
Not covered

I did not run any tests or builds, as instructed. The findings were traced in source and not reproduced. I did not deeply read the unit test files (role_contract/package/tests.rs, component_operation/tests.rs, frontend/tests.rs, observatory tests), beyond test names and the comparison fixtures. I read the canic-cli callers (component, info env, admission, frontend capacity) only as far as needed to confirm consequences. CLI output-file creation and the private/public output split were not reviewed. I did not verify whether the external icp CLI checks query-response signatures (this matters for the uncertified-query finding), or whether Fleet Ensure copies infrastructure Candid into `.icp/<env>/canisters` in every deployment mode. For the claim that ic0.canister_version increments on every executed message, I relied on IC specification semantics plus the in-repo evidence of large pre_canister_version values. Root-side handlers were read only to confirm deduplication, the observer rules and the error code behind STATE_UNAVAILABLE. canic-core role_contract::resolve_role_contract and the catalogue internals were not audited.

CLI: fleet, admission, apps, scaffold, network, replica, status, list, inspect, state, token, info, support, output

cli-core2 medium12 low1 info

The cli-core area is the operator front end of the canic binary. `lib.rs` parses the top-level catalog (`cli/help.rs`), forwards `--icp`/`--environment` as hidden per-leaf options through an allowlist (`cli/globals.rs`), and sends everything else to command modules. Those modules parse clap matches and hand off to canic-host workflows right away. Anything that changes IC state (fleet ensure/bootstrap/import, admission, component) goes through a review-then-apply step bound to an exact digest or plan file. Commands that only change local files (app delete, scaffold, fleet generate) use typed confirmation, dry-run, rollback, or create-new/replace-by-digest. `fleet ensure` is the most complex path: before loading the desired document it runs three pre-selectors (clean reinstall, completed reset, completed preparation), then a funding, operator-mint or plan/apply branch. A threaded progress/receipt layer renders sanitized live output and writes bounded 0600 JSONL timing receipts. Overall quality is high. Digests are strictly validated, next-step commands are shell-quoted, admission plans are re-derived and checked against live state, delete targets are canonicalized, and no secret ever passes through argv or logs. I found no critical or high defect in these paths. The main risks are about consistency, not authority: - **Environment defaults in fleet ensure.** The three pre-selectors use three different environment defaults. The same logical invocation can go to a different reset/reinstall workflow depending on whether `--environment` is typed. Without it, completed-source flows fall through to paths that decode predecessor records. - **info list fan-out.** It starts one OS thread and several icp subprocesses per registry entry, with no bound. - **Workspace members.** `app create` and `app delete` do not maintain the workspace `members` list. The remaining findings are diagnostic, UX and docs defects: missing-role detection that never fires, colliding `info env` variable names, a stub `inspect canister` used as the first help example, a replica stop that can start a replica while probing, inconsistent usage-error exit codes and discarded clap diagnostics, silent `--out` overwrites, silently dropped global options, unsanitized canister strings in `inspect`/`info list`, and a broken first-App sequence in INSTALLING.md and the operator walkthrough. Destructive commands in this area do require explicit approval and default to the local network, except `fleet ensure`, which takes its environment from the desired document. Help pages stay within three examples, and command lists are ASCII-sorted in declarations and dispatch. The hard-coded group usages for admission, info and token advertise a `help` subcommand that exits nonzero.

Strengths
  • Every IC-mutating CLI path is two-step and digest-bound. `parse_digest` accepts only 64 lowercase hex characters (crates/canic-cli/src/fleet/mod.rs:1330). Apply paths re-read retained authority rather than trusting argv (fleet/mod.rs:565-576, fleet/bootstrap/mod.rs:96-114, fleet/import/mod.rs:118-127, component/mod.rs:106-118).
  • Next-step commands are single-quote shell-escaped, include `--environment`, `--icp` and `--identity`, and do not echo attacker text unquoted (fleet/mod.rs:624-645, fleet/completed_reset/mod.rs:225-238, fleet/bootstrap/mod.rs:128-139).
  • Fleet progress output removes control characters from Root-supplied component strings, bounds every line to terminal width, and restores the alternate screen from an async-signal-safe handler and a panic hook (fleet/progress/render/mod.rs:319-324, fleet/progress/terminal/mod.rs:22-55,117-134).
  • Timing receipts are created with create_new and mode 0600, capped at 8 MiB per file and 64 KiB per event, and a display failure can never change a paid-work decision (fleet/progress/receipt/mod.rs:24-25,98-138,230-254; fleet/progress/mod.rs:319-329).
  • Admission apply checks a lot before sending: the plan file uses deny_unknown_fields; on apply the CLI re-derives the successor policy, participant-catalog digest and operation id; it re-checks the live Registry, admission status and Root catalogs; and it verifies that the Coordinator response matches the plan (admission/mod.rs:183-203,316-345,589-715).
  • `app delete` accepts only a canonical, non-symlink directory strictly under the apps root, requires the exact app name typed interactively, and offers --dry-run (apps/mod.rs:370-490).
  • Scaffold writes are validated against a TOML reparse of the workspace manifest, and a failed scaffold restores original documents and removes the new directory, with a typed error if rollback itself fails (scaffold/mod.rs:441-519,541-589).
  • Global options are forwarded only once, conflicts with hidden leaf options are rejected, and a global flag placed after the command is rejected with a typed clap error (cli/globals.rs:66-146; lib.rs:211-244).
Not covered

I did not trace host workflows beyond the CLI selection points (clean_reinstall, completed_reset, completed_preparation, plan_reinstall internals, capacity import journal, operator-mint execution); those belong to other units. I read test files only where they settled a hypothesis (fleet/tests.rs head, tests.rs, inspect tests). I skimmed fleet/progress/receipt/summary, fleet/startup_funding (second half), apps/render (second half), and list/tests.rs, scaffold/tests.rs and replica/tests.rs only lightly. Following the read-only rules I executed nothing: clap parse behaviour was confirmed by reading the clap_builder 4.6.7 source, and cargo's behaviour for non-member packages (finding on app create/delete) comes from known cargo semantics, not a run. The fd-exhaustion and thread-panic scenario in the info list finding is inferred from code and platform limits, not measured. Modules outside the assigned paths (auth, backup, restore, cycles, medic, metrics, endpoints, blob_storage, build, evidence) were not reviewed.

CLI: cycles, auth, medic, metrics, endpoints, evidence, info subnets

cli-ops4 medium7 low

This unit covers the operator-facing ops commands in canic-cli. `cycles` has three kinds of command. `balance`, `mint` and `transfer` pass straight through to `icp cycles`, with Canic resolving `<fleet>/<role>` receivers. `topup` is limited to the Coordinator or one exact current Root. `convert` asks a Root to turn its ICP into cycles and keeps a local pending-operation journal so the same operation id is reused on retry. `funding` is a read-only diagnostic that checks Registry, Coordinator and Root status against each other. `info cycles` and `info metrics` fan out observations to every canister. `auth` only covers renewal status: the CLI issues and stores no tokens. `medic` builds a pass/warn/fail readiness report from local ensure state plus optional live probes (admission, auth renewal, blob storage). `evidence` compares envelopes and runs policy gates. `info subnets` builds an all-or-nothing inventory from Coordinator and Root evidence. Quality is generally high. Journalling is correct (flock, temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync). Responses are typed and bound to their operation id, parsing uses checked arithmetic, and diagnostic reports are strict about agreeing with each other. I found no critical or high defects. The main risks are operator-facing mistakes rather than protocol breaks: - `cycles transfer <fleet>/<role>` sends cycles to the target canister's Cycles Ledger account. Canic workload canisters have no code to spend that balance, so the cycles get stuck, even though the help text presents this as a normal way to fund a target. - The convert journal can silently replay a completed conversion instead of running a new one, and nothing in `--json` output shows it. - `cycles funding` always fails for a Fleet that has ever removed a Root, because it does not skip Removed Registry entries. - Medic's auth-renewal check reports Ready while renewal is disabled or failing, so CI stays green until the proof expires. - A missing local Candid file for the issuer is misdiagnosed as an unregistered issuer, and medic then recommends reinstalling the dependency closure, which wipes application state. Scaling is a secondary concern. `info cycles` and `info metrics` start one OS thread per canister with no cap (Fleets allow up to 4096 canisters). Each thread runs several `icp` subprocesses, most of them update calls through Root. That can exhaust thread or process limits, since `thread::spawn` panics on failure, and can trigger rate limiting as Fleets grow. Several commands also require a single Fleet Subnet Root and do not work on multi-Root Fleets.

Strengths
  • The convert pending journal writes intent before the effect under an exclusive flock. Writes are atomic (temp file with create_new, fsync, rename, directory fsync), and concurrent reservations are covered by a test (crates/canic-cli/src/cycles/convert/pending.rs:119-199, 268-327, 449-485).
  • Refill command and status responses are decoded as typed Candid and bound to the expected operation id; mismatches are typed errors (crates/canic-cli/src/cycles/convert/response.rs:72-127).
  • Top-up targets are limited to the Coordinator or an exact Root principal that is in the current topology. The cycle amount parser rejects zero and overflow via checked_mul (crates/canic-cli/src/cycles/wallet.rs:371-399, 542-570, 689-695).
  • Funding diagnostics check terminal ensure authority, the live Registry, Coordinator status and each Root's status against each other before rendering anything (crates/canic-cli/src/cycles/funding.rs:381-497).
  • `info subnets` produces no partial report. It validates authority, revision, content hash, Root order, duplicate or missing summaries, and uses checked counts (crates/canic-cli/src/info_subnets/model.rs:98-301).
  • A panicking worker thread becomes an explicit per-canister error row instead of aborting the report (crates/canic-cli/src/cycles/transport.rs:144-166; crates/canic-cli/src/metrics/transport.rs:103-114).
  • The auth issuer principal is canonicalised before it is put into a Candid argument, and the local Candid method must be declared as a query (crates/canic-cli/src/auth/codec.rs:30-36, 140-142; crates/canic-cli/src/auth/mod.rs:682-710).
Not covered

I did not independently verify icp-cli 1.x behaviour: whether `icp cycles transfer` accepts suffixes like "4T" and whether `canister top-up` deduplicates. The transfer finding relies on Canic's own docs for the Cycles Ledger semantics. I followed call paths into these modules only far enough to confirm hypotheses, not a full review: - canic-host observability - the root InspectCanister/ObserveCanister costs - the completed-estate ledger reconciliation - admission collect_status - blob_storage medic_summary - support/registry_tree - the output module I did not review policy_gate evaluation internals in canic-host. No tests were run (read-only mandate). The auth path contains no token issuance or storage code; `canic auth` only exposes `renewal status`, so the token-issuance focus question does not apply to this unit.

Backup crate: restore planning, apply and runner, execution

backup-restore2 high3 medium4 low

This unit is the host-side restore pipeline (plan, then dry-run, then apply journal, then native runner) plus the backup capture runner and its execution journal. A restore plan is built from a validated manifest and an optional mapping, with every derived projection checked again. The dry-run lays the work out in fixed phases: upload all snapshots, stop all members parent-first, load all, start all child-first, then run member and deployment verification. The runner claims one operation at a time. Each claim is journalled as Pending before its effect runs. Uploads first record the target's snapshot inventory, and command-lifetime locks catch orphaned child processes. After an interruption, stop and start are reconciled from `canister status`, uploads from the before/after inventory difference, and loads are replayed only while the target is proven stopped. Terminal state and its receipt are published together in one durable write. The backup runner mirrors this and adds failure containment: after a failed step it restarts the canisters it stopped. Engineering quality is high. The code fails closed on malformed journals, re-checks artifact checksums over the exact private copy before upload, and uses typed errors throughout. The crash-point test harness (barrier-killed child processes) is unusually thorough. The main risks are not in the journalling mechanics but in what those mechanics assume about the platform and the fleet. First, upload reconciliation treats any single new snapshot as the completed upload. An interrupted or failed upload leaves a partially uploaded snapshot (metadata written, data chunks unfinished), and that snapshot gets adopted and later loaded. Second, backup failure containment restarts the fleet but keeps snapshots that were already taken, so a retried backup mixes two separate stop windows into one manifest that claims crash consistency. Third, nothing ever deletes the snapshots that backup creates or restore uploads. They keep billing storage and eventually hit the per-canister snapshot limit. The strict reconciliation baseline then cannot recover from the operator's natural fix, which is deleting an old snapshot. Other gaps: a restore is never bound to the current release, topology or network. The restore runner has no pre-mutation authority preflight and no containment or abort path. Backup snapshot creation does not re-check that the target is still stopped. Journal rewrite and validation cost grows quadratically. None of these needed a test run to establish; each is traced in code. Findings that depend on how the IC treats partially uploaded snapshots are marked medium confidence.

Strengths
  • Intent before effect: each operation is claimed Pending, and an upload's pre-effect snapshot inventory is durably written before the external command runs (crates/canic-backup/src/restore/runner/execute.rs:210-222).
  • Terminal state and receipt are committed in one validated durable replacement. On read, the latest receipt must match the operation's terminal state and timestamp (execute.rs:796-816, restore/runner/io.rs:44-82).
  • Upload artifacts are copied into a private 0700 staging directory with no-follow opens, and the checksum is computed over the copied bytes and verified before the upload command sees the path, which closes TOCTOU swaps (restore/runner/artifact.rs:89-158, artifacts/secure.rs:124-138).
  • LoadSnapshot requires fresh proof that the target is stopped. Precondition and observation failures are recorded durably as typed failed receipts rather than guessed (restore/runner/precondition.rs:18-40, execute.rs:322-375).
  • Post-restore verification requires Running status and a matching module hash, normalized for 0x prefixes and case (execute.rs:414-435).
  • Command-lifetime locks inherited by child processes block replay while an orphaned icp child or its descendants are still running (persistence/command_lifetime_lock/mod.rs:45-89, execute.rs:663-691).
  • Persisted plans are fully re-validated: principals, hashes, fixed-identity remap, duplicate targets, canonical parent-first ordering and every summary projection are recomputed and compared (restore/plan/validation.rs:24-162).
  • Backup failure containment restarts every canister it stopped when a later step fails, and reconciles a failed stop from authoritative status first (runner/mod.rs:317-522).
Not covered

I did not deep-read the internals of artifacts/secure.rs (no-follow copy and hash), the persistence durable-write and flock primitives, backup plan/preflight authority construction (plan/preflight/*), CLI option parsing, or the host icp process runner. The IC and icp-cli behaviour for partially uploaded snapshots (whether they are listed and whether they can be loaded) cannot be settled from repository code; the gate report only probed successful uploads. Per instructions I ran no tests or builds. Test files were read only for intent. For the performance finding, the real size of icp command output is estimated, not measured.

Backup crate: persistence and locks, plan, journal, manifest, artifacts, discovery; CLI backup and restore commands

backup-persistence1 high2 medium10 low1 info

This unit is the host-side persistence layer of canic-backup and the `canic backup` / `canic restore` CLI commands. BackupLayout (persistence/layout.rs) owns four JSON documents: backup plan, execution journal, download journal and manifest. Mutable documents are replaced by writing and fsyncing a sibling temp file, renaming it over the target and fsyncing the directory. The manifest is create-only: it is published with hard_link and an existing copy is adopted only if it is byte-identical. Mutation is serialized with flock sidecar locks, and a per-command lifetime lock proves child processes have exited. Artifacts are hashed through descriptor-relative O_NOFOLLOW traversal. A snapshot directory is published by fsyncing every file and directory, re-hashing, then renameat with NOREPLACE. The integrity checks bind manifest to download journal and plan to execution journal. The CLI adds list, reference resolution, prune, verify, status and inspect, plus restore plan, prepare, run and status on top of these primitives. The low-level primitives are good quality: locks resist symlinks and are released when the holder dies, writes are atomic, traversal cannot escape the root, restore staging hashes the exact bytes it copies, serde is strict, and the crash-barrier tests are thorough. The main defects are in how the pieces are composed. `backup prune` only looks at backup status, so it can delete a backup directory that holds an unfinished restore journal and its staged artifacts. That strands a production restore with its target canisters stopped and no journal to reconcile. Numeric backup references are positions in a list that shifts whenever any backup attempt starts, and `restore run <N> --execute` re-resolves the number on every call. It can therefore execute a different prepared restore than the one the operator meant. Several defects in the live backup runner are currently hidden because the CLI executor always fails preflight on purpose (create/executor/mod.rs:45-53). Each becomes serious once that stub is replaced. - Relative `--out` paths are handed to an `icp` child process whose working directory is the workspace root, while canic pre-creates the empty temp directory relative to its own working directory. This can produce a verified backup that contains no data. - The finalize manifest's `created_at` is non-deterministic, so an interrupted finalize can never re-adopt its own manifest, and the backup is stuck on ManifestConflict. - The runner hashes artifacts with a traversal that rejects `./` and `../` paths and any symlinked ancestor, which covers /tmp and /var on macOS. The layout then fails permanently after the paid snapshot operations have already run. Existing unit tests using std::env::temp_dir() cannot pass on macOS; CI is Ubuntu-only. Lower-severity issues: - The preflight time limit (TTL) is never rechecked after acceptance. - `backup create` writes the plan and journal before taking the journal lock. - Prune retention does not verify the backups it keeps. - JSON reads are unbuffered, costing one syscall per byte. - Manifest artifact-path validation is inconsistent with the path resolver used at restore time. - Hash case handling is inconsistent between validation and comparison. - Directory creation is not made durable in the parent directory. - The docs advertise live backup, which currently always fails preflight.

Strengths
  • Sidecar file locks: symlinks and special files are rejected before open, the file is opened O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC and its type re-checked with fstat, and a non-blocking flock is taken. The lock releases on process death with no stale-lock cleanup needed, and tests kill the lock owner (crates/canic-backup/src/persistence/file_lock/mod.rs:40-67, journal_lock/mod.rs:146-195).
  • The command-lifetime lock proves an external command and all its descendants have exited: the fd is inherited, the owner closes it, then probes until it can reacquire (crates/canic-backup/src/persistence/command_lifetime_lock/mod.rs:71-90).
  • Artifact publication fsyncs every file and directory, re-hashes from the synced descriptors, verifies the expected checksum, publishes with renameat NOREPLACE, fsyncs the parent, and has an explicit recovery branch for trees already published (crates/canic-backup/src/persistence/artifact_commit.rs:100-146).
  • Secure traversal opens each component relative to its parent fd with O_NOFOLLOW and re-checks the type with fstat. Restore staging hashes the exact bytes it copies, so the upload source cannot be swapped after verification (crates/canic-backup/src/artifacts/secure.rs:124-175, 302-313).
  • Durable JSON writes use a unique sibling temp file, fsync, rename and a directory fsync. The manifest is create-only via hard_link, with exact adoption and rejection of symlinked entries (crates/canic-backup/src/persistence/json.rs:47-114, persistence/layout.rs:76-124).
  • Serde contracts are strict: deny_unknown_fields everywhere, required_option for nullable-but-required fields, and plan, journal and manifest versions all pinned to 1, matching the pre-1.0 v1 policy (crates/canic-backup/src/serialization.rs, journal/types.rs, manifest/types.rs, plan/types.rs).
  • Artifact paths are confined to the backup root where they are used: Normal-only path resolution, and restore canonicalizes the root and rejects a symlinked root (crates/canic-backup/src/persistence/integrity/path.rs:11-27, restore/apply/mod.rs:215-233).
  • The live backup CLI fails closed rather than faking authority proof while Coordinator-backed preflight is missing (crates/canic-cli/src/backup/create/executor/mod.rs:45-53, 133-138).
Not covered

I did not independently review the runner and execution state machines (crates/canic-backup/src/runner, crates/canic-backup/src/execution) or restore planning, apply and runner internals. I read them only as far as needed to confirm or refute persistence and CLI hypotheses. I could not confirm whether `icp canister snapshot download --output` creates a missing output directory, which decides whether finding 3 is silent data loss or a loud failure after effects. Non-unix (Windows) behaviour was assessed only as "unsupported". I ran no tests (read-only task); the macOS O_NOFOLLOW/ENOTDIR behaviour was confirmed with a read-only Python openat probe on this host. I only skimmed the CLI test suites, backup/model.rs, render/*.rs, restore/error.rs, and the persistence operational_readiness tests other than manifest_publication and download_effect.

canic facade crate: public API, non-endpoint macros, testing helpers, features and dependency closure

facade9 low3 info

The `canic` facade is a thin re-export and macro crate. `lib.rs` exposes curated `api`, `access`, `dto`, `ids`, `protocol`, `diagnostics` and `fleet_admission` modules over `canic-core` and the optional `canic-control-plane`. It also exposes a doc-hidden `__internal`, which re-exports all of `canic_core` for macro expansion, and a host-only `__build` of build-script helpers. The `build!` macro runs in role build scripts. It validates package metadata and `canic.toml`, writes the per-role runtime authority and root config sources into OUT_DIR, and sets `canic_*` cfg flags from the role's capabilities. The lifecycle macros (`start!`, `start_local!`, `start_wasm_store!`, `start_fleet_root!`, `start_fleet_coordinator!`, `finish!`) connect IC `init`/`post_upgrade` to core adapters and schedule application hooks on zero-delay timers. `canic::testing` holds the PocketIC qualification helpers. It builds only for non-wasm targets with the `testing` feature, and it embeds a prebuilt stand-in Root wasm. Quality is generally high. Dependency boundaries are clean: TOML, `ic-testkit` and `build_support` are target-gated to the host, and none of them can reach canister wasm. The host checks the exact Canic feature set so features cannot slip in through Cargo unification, and it rejects renamed dependencies, which matches the macros' hard-coded `::canic` paths. The capability-to-cfg mapping in `build!` is an exhaustive match. Lifecycle participants are type-checked, `finish!` is enforced at compile time, and generated sources are written without following symlinks. The most significant risk is in `start.rs`. The application's one-time install hook (`canic_setup` then `canic_install(args)`) is scheduled only as a heap timer, in the same message that makes the Prepared-to-Active transition and deletes the durable application init args. If that timer traps, or an upgrade lands before it runs, application initialization is lost for good. Neither an upgrade nor a retried ConfigureRuntime runs it again, although the runtime docs say activation must expose an explicit retry path. The remaining findings are low or info: a facade `perf!` macro that cannot compile, and hazards with unbounded perf checkpoint labels. The generated standalone config fallback cannot work with `start_local!`. The supported API exposes root-only mutation entry points and leaves gaps in the `ids` re-exports. A 1 MB prebuilt fixture wasm has no freshness check. The feature and auth docs are stale.

Strengths
  • Host-only code is strictly target-gated: `build_support`/`__build` (crates/canic/src/lib.rs:20-21,71-83), `testing` (lib.rs:30-31) and the `toml`/`ic-testkit` dependencies (crates/canic/Cargo.toml:44-46; crates/canic-core/Cargo.toml:57-62). No TOML parser or PocketIC code can reach canister wasm.
  • `build!` maps every `RoleCapabilityKey` to a cfg in an exhaustive match with no wildcard (crates/canic/src/macros/build.rs:176-233). The same `CANIC_CUSTOM_CFG_NAMES` catalog is shared by the facade build.rs and downstream expansions (build_support/cfg_catalog.rs; crates/canic/build.rs), so adding a capability forces the cfg to be updated.
  • `write_build_source_if_changed` refuses symlinked outputs and leaves unchanged files untouched (crates/canic/src/build_support/config.rs:76-98). Wasm builds must carry the host role-contract marker (config.rs:106-112).
  • Lifecycle participants are compile-time checked as exact `fn() -> ()` pairs, with compile_fail doctests for partial and async declarations (crates/canic/src/macros/start.rs:8-18,563-580). A missing `finish!` is a compile error through a marker const (start.rs:494-517).
  • Macro paths are consistent with host policy: the host rejects a renamed or optional `canic` dependency (crates/canic-host/src/role_contract/package/mod.rs:963-996) and requires the package-selected feature set to equal the declared closure exactly (mod.rs:850-878), so hard-coded `::canic` paths and feature cfgs stay sound.
  • `fleet_admission::require_caller` is synchronous and fails closed. It delegates to a phase-checked projection lookup that refuses anything not Open (crates/canic/src/fleet_admission/mod.rs:12-14; crates/canic-core/src/workflow/fleet_admission_projection/mod.rs:94-101).
  • The testing fixtures derive synthetic identities from domain-separated hashes, reject ambiguous Component occurrences, validate role artifacts against the topology, and use checked arithmetic for revisions and counts (crates/canic/src/testing/managed_app/mod.rs:412-430; managed_component_group/mod.rs:487-506,1005-1053).
Not covered

Not reviewed in depth: the endpoint macro bodies (crates/canic/src/macros/endpoints/role.rs, root.rs, wasm_store.rs, fleet_coordinator.rs, blob_storage*.rs), read only at the call sites I needed. Also not reviewed: the canic-macros proc-macro implementation (only its Cargo.toml), and core or control-plane internals beyond confirming hypotheses tied to the facade. Nothing was compiled or executed. The claims that `canic::perf!` fails to compile and that `start_local!` traps with the standalone config come from reading macro and code logic and have not been reproduced. Not assessed: how host `cargo tree` feature evidence treats dev-dependency `testing` features, PocketIC behaviour with synthetic 29-byte principals, the actual wasm-size cost of the embedded root ConfigModel, and ic-testkit internals. I checked for wire drift between the embedded `sharding_root_stub.wasm` and current DTOs only by git history (no dto rpc/capability/error changes since it was built), not by rebuilding.

Canisters, apps, test crates, Makefile, scripts and CI

tests-ci1 medium12 low2 info

This unit covers the machinery that decides what gets tested and released: the GitHub workflows (ci.yml, security.yml), the Makefile, the governed workspace test runner (scripts/ci/run-workspace-tests.sh plus its TSV inventory), the PocketIC worker launcher, the release and publish scripts, the pinned tool installers, and the test crates canic-testing-internal and canic-tests, plus the canisters/ and apps/ test fixtures. CI runs on every pull request and every push to main. The jobs are preflight/security, then MSRV and checks (fmt, clippy, feature matrix), then separate ordinary and PocketIC lanes, plus a release-profile build for commits whose message starts with "Release ". Releases are cut locally: `make validate`, a transactional version bump, commit and tag, then one atomic push. Publishing to crates.io is a separate manual step. Engineering quality is high for a shell-heavy pipeline. Actions are pinned by SHA, every downloaded binary is checked against a digest, every script uses set -euo pipefail, and scratch deletion is tightly scoped. The integration-test inventory is guarded, the runner tests itself with fake cargo and pocket-ic binaries, and the release flow checks that the remote is an ancestor and that the tag is free before changing versions. The main weaknesses are in test soundness, not script safety. Several classes of tests look like coverage but never run in any lane: `#[test]` functions in governed-feature-only modules that are missing from the registry, canic-host `local-fleet` tests, and every doctest, including the compile_fail contracts. The serial PocketIC lanes use name filters and never check that at least one test ran. A routine rename would turn the whole governed catalogue (about 60 recovery, funding and conservation journeys) into a silent 0-test pass. Some static guards are weaker than they claim. trap_guard does not see the `ic_cdk::trap` spelling, and at least 10 such calls sit outside the approved boundaries (7 of them outside the lifecycle dir and the IC-ops facade). The release tooling has smaller gaps. The `release-commit` recipe tags even when `git commit` fails, so the tag can land on the wrong commit. canic-core is still published with a `--no-verify` whose original reason no longer applies. The release-candidate and index guards check only file paths, so any Cargo.toml or Cargo.lock content change passes. The fast lane can ship lockfile dependency bumps without running any tests. On main, cancel-in-progress can cancel a release commit's CI, which contradicts the governance claim that each release commit gets one complete CI result. None of these can cause cycle loss or a controller takeover. They weaken the evidence that release gates are meant to provide.

Strengths
  • All external Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs; checkouts set persist-credentials: false; the workflow token is `contents: read`; every job has a timeout. check-release-integrity-contract.sh:66-101 enforces all of this.
  • Every downloaded tool is bound to a digest in tool-versions.env. PocketIC is checked at both the archive and the binary level, and a cached or caller-supplied POCKET_IC_BIN is re-checked before use (install-pocketic.sh:35-49, check-pocketic-version-alignment.sh:46-53, verify-file-checksum.sh).
  • check-workspace-test-inventory.sh:25-98 requires every top-level integration target to appear exactly once in the inventory, with a valid lane and no target name spanning two selection classes, so Cargo `--test` name collisions cannot move a target between lanes.
  • test-workspace-test-runner.sh drives the real runner with fake cargo and pocket-ic binaries. It checks barrier ordering, fail-fast behaviour, quiet output with retained diagnostics, and server cleanup for every failure stage.
  • The release transaction is careful. Validation receipts are bound to the exact HEAD (run-release-validation-lane.sh:19-53); bump-version.sh:83-111 rolls back through a tar backup on ERR/INT/TERM; check-release-remote-state.sh checks remote ancestry and that the tag is free before any version change and again before push; push-release.sh:17-19 pushes branch and tag in one atomic push.
  • Scratch deletion is tightly scoped. The path is regex-validated, must be a direct child of .tmp and must not be a symlink before rm -rf. PocketIC kills target only processes whose --port-file lies inside the owned scratch (cleanup-release-artifacts.sh:39-80, stop-owned-pocketic-servers.sh:29-56).
  • run-validation-targets.sh:9-22 runs from a private copy of itself that has passed `bash -n`, so a concurrent edit cannot splice new shell into a long run. Pipelines use pipefail so make/tee/annotate failures are not lost.
  • The security gates fail closed. The Gitleaks scan covers full history and refuses shallow clones and config overrides (run-secret-scan.sh:22-51). The dependency-risk gate blocks on vulnerabilities, yanked or unsound crates, and unmaintained direct dependencies, and a weekly scheduled workflow re-runs it (check-dependency-risk-inventory.sh:67-114).
Not covered

I did not read in depth the bodies of the large PocketIC journeys: most of the 17.5k-line fleet_registry/baseline.rs, native_agent_delegation.rs, timer_authority.rs, pic_blob_storage.rs, icydb_lifecycle_composition.rs, fixture_provisioning/**, and instruction_audit_support/**. I also did not read the probe canisters' logic (runtime_probe, blob_storage_probe, cycles_ledger_stub, icp_refill_stub) beyond their manifests and entry points. Among the scripts, I skipped the wasm audit, ablation and instruction-audit reports, the doc-guard scripts, verify-packaged-downstream-*.sh past the packaging helpers, and I read check-release-integrity-contract.sh only in part. I could not assess whether ic-testkit's sealed artifact cache soundly invalidates restored target/test-artifacts caches, because that lives in a sibling repo. Per the read-only rules I ran no builds or tests. So the claim that libtest passes on zero matched tests rests on known libtest/cargo behaviour, and how often CI runs get cancelled is inferred from commit timestamps.

Security across trust boundaries (cross-cutting)

xc-security2 medium5 low

Canic enforces caller authority at the endpoint boundary. Generated endpoints either run a compiled `requires(...)` access expression, or, for the role-owned command unions (`canic_root_command`, `canic_command`, `canic_coordinator_command`, `canic_wasm_store_command`), are emitted as `internal, public` and run inline checks per variant before dispatch. I enumerated every command variant on root, managed, coordinator and store canisters. Each one currently gets an explicit check: controller, exact coordinator, registered component member or parent, parent/root/child topology, or a custom predicate. The cryptographic trust chain for delegated tokens and role attestations is complete and fails closed. It checks the root chain-key batch proof against the configured key and policy fields, the issuer canister signature against canister id and seed, cert and claims hashing, Fleet audience, role grants, presenter==caller, and for attestations the subject, audience, subnet and epoch. Controller mutations follow an observe-then-set pattern with exact expected controller sets. Host-side identity handling, subprocess spawning, backup path traversal and CI tool downloads are careful. The main risks are about who can obtain authority, not about forging it. The public `PrepareDelegatedToken` path, which is by design an open login surface, mints tokens for any caller, including the anonymous principal. The proof-bearing `auth::authenticated()` lane then accepts those tokens. The session lane explicitly rejects anonymous and infrastructure subjects. The same public path signs caller-chosen `ext` bytes and self-issuable declared application scopes. The contracts describe both as issuer-controlled or not self-grantable, so apps that follow the docs can be spoofed. The public issuance and session surfaces also have fixed global capacities (512 retained preparations per issuer, 2048 sessions per verifier). Any actor can fill them using free self-authenticating principals. The ingress `inspect_message` hooks filter only by payload size and decodability, never by caller. As a result, controller-only command methods on root, the Fleet Coordinator (which holds the treasury) and the wasm store accept megabyte-scale ingress from anonymous senders, and the receiving canister pays the induction cost. Lower-severity structural issues: the per-variant command authorization is a hand-maintained, fail-open classification. Denials of unauthenticated requests write persistent log entries that anyone can use to evict audit history. Explicit pool import wipes a target without observing it first, and does not exclude in-flight allocations.

Strengths
  • Delegated-token verification is end-to-end and fails closed. It checks the chain-key root proof against the configured public key, key id, derivation path and key version (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/delegated/chain_key.rs:419-440), and the issuer canister signature against canister id and seed (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/issuer_canister_sig.rs:224-247). It also enforces cert-hash binding, Fleet audience, role-grant subset and presenter==caller (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/delegated/verify.rs:207-265). Builds without the crypto feature return Err rather than skipping verification (chain_key.rs:244-252).
  • The positive verification cache key binds the proof hash, claims hash, issuer-proof digest and caller, and every cache hit re-runs all semantic checks (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/delegated/cache.rs:33-65, crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/token/verification.rs:109-127).
  • Local-subnet role attestation binds subject==caller, audience==self, a required subnet==live subnet, and epoch floors (crates/canic-core/src/ops/auth/verify/mod.rs:20-90). Issuance checks the subject, role and placement subnet against the registered member binding (crates/canic-core/src/workflow/runtime/auth/prepare/admission.rs:44-80).
  • Controller changes use observe-then-set with exact expected sets and refuse unexpected live controllers (crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/fleet_subnet_root.rs:193-236; pool reinspection uses has_exact_root_controllers at crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/canister_pool/mod.rs:656-663).
  • Root funding acceptance authenticates the exact protected Coordinator, rejects anonymous, and accepts exactly the validated grant or traps before commit (crates/canic-control-plane/src/workflow/root_funding/mod.rs:41-48, 189-215).
  • Host secret handling: the exported PEM is captured as bytes, zeroed after parsing, cross-checked against the active principal, and never placed in diagnostics (crates/canic-host/src/icp/run.rs:24-42, crates/canic-host/src/icp/management.rs:203-224). Production subprocesses use argv without shell interpolation.
  • Backup artifact traversal opens each path component with openat plus O_NOFOLLOW and rejects any component that is not a normal name (crates/canic-backup/src/artifacts/secure.rs:140-172).
  • CI tool installers download over HTTPS only and verify pinned SHA-256 checksums (scripts/ci/install-icp-cli.sh:53-55, scripts/ci/install-pocketic.sh:36-47, scripts/ci/install-binaryen.sh:47-54).
Not covered

Not covered: the host fleet-ensure workflows in depth (crates/canic-host/src/fleet_ensure/ops/platform.rs is about 10k lines; I read only the delete effect and the identity and agent setup). Backup and restore semantics, including manifest-to-target canister binding and snapshot upload checks. Funding-policy bounds for child RequestCycles and for root placement and provisioning capabilities (checked only at the caller-authorization layer). Blob-storage billing and Cashier trust. ICRC-21 consent. Cost bounds of root chain-key ECDSA signing. Cycle-safety of pool recycle and reset. I did not run cargo audit or any build or test. The IC ingress-induction fee figures used for the ingress finding are from IC pricing documentation and were not measured.

Contract conformance (cross-cutting)

xc-contracts1 medium8 low3 info

This lens checked code against the normative documents across crates: AGENTS.md, docs/contracts, the architecture and feature docs, CONFIG.md, the 0.110 design and governance. Canic mostly follows its mechanical rules. Every product schema, journal and stable key is still at v1, and the pre-1.0 hard-cut guard backs this with a self-tested fixture. No `#[path]` is used and `#[allow]` is rare and justified. Command and request DTOs do not derive Default. export()/import() is used only on *Data snapshots. The TOML and YAML parsers stay out of canister wasm: the config is rendered to Rust, Root embeds only the TOML text, and YAML parsing lives in one host module. The CLI top-level catalog and dispatch are ASCII-sorted, and a recursive test checks help ordering and the three-example cap. canic-core's policy and model layers are pure and are protected by self-tested layering guards. The main weaknesses sit at crate and document boundaries. First, the layering guards only scan canic-core. As a result canic-control-plane, which holds the most privileged Root and Coordinator logic, breaks rules those guards enforce: stable records are built from ~30 public Request/Response DTOs, ops call policy decision functions, and one ops function spans two awaits. Second, the delegated-token documentation contradicts itself and the code. CONFIG.md calls the IC root key optional, the schema rustdoc says otherwise, and runtime requires it for build_network="ic". Build-time validation does not enforce it, so a mainnet config written from the docs builds cleanly and then traps at verifier init. Third, the build-network class is fail-open. It defaults to Local when ICP_ENVIRONMENT is unset or the icp.yaml network is custom, and that relaxes the NNS subnet-binding checks. Fourth, the Root command endpoint authenticates through non-exhaustive `matches!` allowlists, so a new variant is public by default. The remaining findings are contract drift. Two normative documents disagree about Cargo cleanup after release. A Project identity survives in the evidence-gate schema and report. Anti-resurrection tests exist even though AGENTS.md forbids them. Two modules keep both foo.rs and foo/. Admission authority validation uses long mixed &&/|| expressions. The crate README, lib.rs and the recurring layer audit describe a linear policy-to-ops chain that AGENTS.md forbids, and ACCESS_ARCHITECTURE.md is stale.

Strengths
  • Pre-1.0 hard-cut enforcement is executable and self-tested: scripts/ci/check-pre-1-0-hard-cut.sh:6-7 rejects >v1 product schema constants and migration readers, with fixture self-test at lines 20-30. Every *_SCHEMA_VERSION/*_VERSION constant in crates is 1 (e.g. crates/canic-core/src/state_contract.rs:44, crates/canic-host/src/fleet_ensure/model/mod.rs:24).
  • TOML/YAML parsers are kept out of canister wasm. crates/canic-core/Cargo.toml and crates/canic/Cargo.toml put toml under cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32")). parse_toml is cfg-gated (crates/canic-core/src/config/mod.rs:197). Config is rendered to Rust (crates/canic-core/src/bootstrap/render.rs). Only Root embeds the TOML text (crates/canic/src/macros/start.rs:384). serde-saphyr is used only in crates/canic-host/src/icp_config/manifest/mod.rs.
  • canic-core layering holds and is guarded. domain/policy has no ops, storage, async, IC or serialization imports, and model has no ops or workflow calls. scripts/ci/run-layering-guards.sh self-tests its detectors against fixtures.
  • Data-shape conventions are consistent. No Default on command/request DTOs in crates/*/src/dto. All export()/import() functions take or return *Data snapshots. Persisted stable-container values end in *Record. Views live under view/.
  • CLI ordering and conciseness contract is tested recursively against rendered help (crates/canic-cli/tests/subcommand_order.rs:5-62). Top-level COMMAND_SPECS and dispatch are ASCII-sorted (crates/canic-cli/src/cli/help.rs:25-122, crates/canic-cli/src/lib.rs:246-270).
  • The stable-memory inventory in docs/features/runtime/stable-memory-layout.md matches the ID constants in crates/canic-core/src/role_contract/allocation.rs exactly. The ranges are enforced by the policy in crates/canic-core/src/memory/policy.rs:320-348.
  • The managed canister command endpoint authenticates inside every arm of an exhaustive match (crates/canic/src/macros/endpoints/role.rs:600-700), so a new variant cannot compile without choosing its auth.
  • Lint suppressions follow the #[expect] preference. The only #![allow] (crates/canic/src/macros/start.rs:521) is a documented false positive. There are zero #[path] module attributes in source.
